name: Amara Ellison
household: Lives with her aunt and two younger cousins in a rented Atlanta duplex. The aunt's evening shift keeps cash tight, and Amara covers the walk home and dinner. A nearby youth arts program is free; travel for programs is not.
school: Large public high school, grade 11. Theater elective and a small writing club; few hands-on tech courses. She drafts on the bus between pickup and homework.
wellbeing: No named concern. She prefers small rehearsal rooms and can skip a loud gym assembly without other support.
motivation: Hear whether a rewritten line lands
Keep a promise to the cousins
See if a low-cost writing program is realistic
strengths: Revises scenes after hearing them aloud
Keeps rehearsals moving when adults are late
Developing: asking for aid information before ruling a program out
workContext: Small indoor group, unhurried, with quiet time to rewrite. No access equipment. Evenings must stay free for caregiving.
constraints: Aid needed to leave the city
narrative: Amara rewrites dialogue for a small church youth play and stays after rehearsal to adjust timing when a scene feels flat. She likes hearing how a line lands. Her aunt's evening shift means Amara walks two cousins home and finishes drafts on the bus. She has no interest in tracking money or repairing gear. She is unsure a writing program away from the city is realistic without aid.

name: Caleb Ruiz-Bennett
household: Shares a house with his mother and uncle on a small equipment lot in a high-desert valley. Cash is limited and the truck is shared. Most repair know-how is local; the library van comes weekly.
school: Small public high school, grade 10. Shop is one semester and often full. No robotics or engineering elective. Internet at home is slow.
wellbeing: Unstated. No support plan. He works better with the shop door open and ear protection he already owns.
motivation: Make a machine run smoother
Be useful on the lot
Avoid a long paid program unless it is clearly worth it
strengths: Notices when a moving part still binds
Keeps informal notes of what he changed
Developing: explaining a repair without a part in hand
workContext: Outdoor or shed shop, self-paced, mostly solo with one experienced adult nearby. Needs reliable transport, not a quiet office.
constraints: Training would require leaving the valley
narrative: Caleb spends Saturdays in his uncle's shed, swapping a mower part and checking whether the blade track runs smoother. He keeps a grease-stained notebook of what he tried. He skips the school paper and has no patience for speeches. Slow internet means he learned by watching repairs. He is unsure leaving the valley for training would be worth the cost.

name: Jordan Hale
household: Two parents and a younger sibling in a modest suburban house. One parent is a payroll clerk. They can cover club fees and a counselor copay, not a private summer research program.
school: Public high school, grade 10. Garden club and an introductory data elective. A counselor gives written step lists when focus slips. Science labs are available but not Jordan's draw.
wellbeing: Focus slips on long verbal directions. School check-ins and written steps help. No interest inference from that support. They still join group discussions they care about.
motivation: Catch a biased sample
Finish a fair comparison
Decide if the interest outlasts one club
strengths: Checks who is missing before graphing
Explains a number pattern to the club
Developing: staying with weeding and other slow physical tasks
workContext: Quiet classroom or library table, moderate pace, small group then solo analysis. Written instructions help. No lift or sensory equipment.
constraints: Aid likely for a four-year campus
narrative: Jordan designs short surveys for the garden club, then checks who never got the form before graphing answers. They like arguing about a biased sample more than weeding. A counselor helps them break tasks into written steps when focus slips. They have no interest in performing or selling. They have not decided whether statistics would stay interesting after the garden project ends.

name: Malik Porter
household: Parents run a small hardware store and live above it with Malik and a sister. The family is busy more than broke. He can use the store computer after close. College would need a mix of wages and aid.
school: Public high school, grade 12. No sports-management class. He built the team sheets himself. Business math is offered; he takes it because the store already uses those habits.
wellbeing: Unstated. No accommodations. He dislikes being pulled into scrimmages and says so.
motivation: Keep a list people can trust
See a delay before it stacks up
Test whether scheduling still appeals off the team
strengths: Reconciles who is actually coming
Updates routes and counts after a change
Developing: saying no when adults treat the list as his hobby
workContext: Sideline table or store counter, steady pace, coordinating people without playing. Standing is fine. Evening games conflict with store close.
narrative: Malik keeps the basketball team's bus times, uniform counts, and who is actually coming, because the coach trusts his lists. He can run the sheet without liking the games much, and he ducks playing when a scrimmage needs bodies. His parents' hardware store gives him practice separating estimates from receipts. He is unsure whether managing schedules would still appeal if it were not tied to a team he already knows.

name: Hanae Park
household: Apartment with both parents and a grandmother. Korean is the home language. Father drives a city bus; mother is a dental receptionist. Expectations for timed math are high; money for private tutoring is not.
school: Public magnet-option high school, grade 10. She chose a heritage-language poetry hour over the science fair. Timed math tests are required. A translation course is not offered until grade 11.
wellbeing: Freezes on timed tests and then rushes. No formal plan yet. Untimed reading she can do. The freeze is not a read on her reasoning.
motivation: Keep a poem's polite tone
Do homework she chose
Tell her family what she actually wants
strengths: Marks where tone shifts between languages
Returns to a clumsy draft
Developing: speaking up about course choices at home
workContext: Quiet desk, slow reading pace, mostly solo with one reader for tone. Timed rooms make the work worse. No other access need.
constraints: Family pressure toward a science track
Timed tests currently shut her down
narrative: Hanae copies short poems between Korean and English and marks where the polite tone disappears. Vocabulary is still thin, so the comparisons feel clumsy, yet she returns to them after homework. Her family expects strong math; she freezes on timed tests and has not said she would rather keep language work than a science track. She is unsure a translation class would still appeal once the poems get harder.

name: Evan Brooks
household: Both parents and a younger brother in a comfortable house. They can pay for clubs, lessons, or a car. Evan has not asked for any of them. No caregiving load.
school: Public high school, grade 11. He meets requirements and skips electives that need an application. A career-day fair was offered; he left early. Shop and robotics were one-time visits.
wellbeing: Unstated. No distress named and no support in place. He is not isolated by rule; he just has not chosen a group.
motivation: Get through the school day
Keep evenings uncomplicated
Leave next year undecided without a fight
strengths: Shows up and finishes required work
Can say clearly that he does not know yet
Developing: trying a second session of anything before dropping it
workContext: No preferred setting yet. He tolerated a quiet classroom more than a loud shop. Pace and people questions are unanswered. No access needs.
narrative: Evan finishes required classes and spends most evenings on short phone clips he rarely posts. Asked what he likes, he says he does not know yet and shrugs at career days. He tried robotics once and shop once and remembers the noise more than the projects. His parents can pay for activities, but he has not found one he would choose again. He is fine leaving next year undecided.

name: Ruby Callahan
household: Family pasture with goats, parents, and a grandfather. Income swings with the season. One shared truck. She does morning feeding before the bus. No nearby college; the community college is 40 minutes away.
school: County public high school, grade 11. Agriculture and a basic biology class. No advanced science. 4-H is the main formal project. Broadband at the house is weak.
wellbeing: Unstated. Early mornings are tiring in kidding season and she still attends. No counselor and no requested accommodation.
motivation: Keep the animals on a steady routine
Notice what changed at the creek
Find training that does not require giving up the herd
strengths: Keeps feeding and milk notes consistent
Compares the bank after rain without rushing
Developing: asking what a campus week would actually cost
workContext: Outdoors, physical, early hours, mostly with family or a small 4-H group. Needs a truck or a program within a bus ride. Fine with mud and weather.
constraints: Aid needed for any campus term
narrative: Ruby checks the creek behind the pasture twice a week, noting muddy banks and which birds stay after rain. She likes the routine of feeding goats more than fair showing and has no interest in ads or performances. The county has no advanced science class, and transport is a shared truck. She wants further training if aid appears, and she is unsure about leaving the animals for a full-time campus.

name: Owen Briggs
household: Both parents and Owen in a modest house. Mother teaches elementary school; father works warehouse nights. Binoculars were a birthday gift. A planetarium trip would need saving. No caregiving.
school: Public middle school, grade 8. General science only. No astronomy club yet. He can use the library after school. Presentations are graded and he dislikes them.
wellbeing: Unstated. He goes quiet when called on. That is about presenting, not a named concern, and he talks readily about the sky notebook at home.
motivation: Compare two explanations of the same sky
Keep the notebook going
Find out if harder math would ruin it
strengths: Copies what he saw before reading an explanation
Stays with a pattern across weeks
Developing: saying an idea out loud in class
workContext: Backyard or quiet library, slow, mostly solo. He can work beside one adult. No access equipment. Loud performances and store floors are a poor fit.
narrative: Owen keeps a backyard sky notebook, sketching where Jupiter sits and copying two explanations when they disagree. He has only binoculars and no science elective yet, so the patterns feel exciting and shaky. He avoids music shows and store work. He likes comparing more than presenting. He does not know whether the interest would hold through harder math.

name: Camila Ortiz
household: Multigenerational apartment above the family restaurant. Spanish and English at home. Lunch service pays bills and her wages. She has little quiet homework time. A community-college kitchen course is a bus ride away.
school: Public high school, grade 12, credit-complete. Food-safety unit was the class she finished carefully. She missed labs when the dinner rush ran long. Counselor knows the work schedule.
wellbeing: Doubles leave her too tired for morning class. She uses a written prep list and a short sit-down break. No diagnosis named. Fatigue is from hours, not from interest.
motivation: Make a recipe repeat
Pass a cooler check
Keep a course possible around night shifts
strengths: Rewrites a checklist after a miss
Tastes and adjusts before service
Developing: protecting a homework hour on delivery nights
workContext: Commercial kitchen, busy at service and quieter at prep. She wants less counter talk. Standing and heat are familiar. Mornings need to stay open after late shifts.
narrative: Camila plates the family restaurant's weekday lunch and rewrites the cooler checklist after a health-inspector note. She likes getting a recipe to taste the same twice and dislikes the rush of explaining specials to a full counter. Evening shifts help the bills and cut into homework. A community-college kitchen course is possible if night hours stay. She is unsure she wants the dining room side even if the cooking stays appealing.

name: Imani Walsh
household: Rental with her mother and a younger brother. Mother works nights at a hospital desk. Imani cooks and locks up. Debate fees are waived. A bachelor's degree depends on aid; a public in-state campus is the working plan.
school: Public high school, grade 12. Debate, U.S. history, and a community-forum assignment. Shop is offered; she does not take it. The library lets her pull local meeting records.
wellbeing: Unstated. She is busy and sleeps after her brother does. No counselor request. She speaks in forums when she has the record in hand.
motivation: Find what a claim actually cites
See who a rule leaves out
Keep college possible while covering dinner
strengths: Lines up conflicting accounts
Rewrites a comment when the wording is unfair
Developing: separating a formal advocate role from a public comment
workContext: Library or meeting room, deadline-driven, with people when there is a text to discuss. Evenings belong to her brother. No access equipment.
narrative: Imani lines up what two articles cite in a local zoning fight before debate practice. She likes finding the record more than scoring points, and she rewrites the club comment when wording leaves renters out. Shop tools do not interest her. Her mother works nights, so Imani handles dinner for a younger brother. She wants a bachelor's if aid holds and is unsure about representing someone in a formal dispute.

name: Mateo Salazar
household: Lives with his mother and shares a room with a cousin. Church and the town hall are the main public rooms. Art supplies are scarce. A city portfolio program would mean a weekly bus he cannot yet pay for.
school: Public high school, grade 11. One art period with limited materials. No drafting course. He is allowed to sketch in the lobby if he stays out of the office.
wellbeing: Fluorescent rooms bring headaches. A window seat and a hat help, and he leaves the cafeteria lights when he can. No further diagnosis stated. Headaches do not limit drawing itself.
motivation: Unblock a door in a crowded room
Try a layout before building it
See whether design study can stay in town
strengths: Tests a path with people actually walking it
Reuses scraps without losing the idea
Developing: describing a layout aloud to a committee
workContext: Daylit table, moderate pace, solo drawing with a short walk-through. Needs a window or other non-fluorescent light. Speaking to a crowd is a poor fit.
narrative: Mateo draws three layouts for the church hall so food tables do not block the side door, then tests the path with a chair. He turns down acting and sales asks. Art class has few materials, so he reuses cardboard. Fluorescent rooms give him headaches, and he works better by a window. He is unsure more design training is possible without city travel.

name: Elise Harper
household: Ranch house with both parents. Land is the asset; cash for tuition is not. Chores are shared. Kits arrive by mail. A state university is several hours away, and she has not stayed overnight off the ranch.
school: Small public high school, grade 12. No electronics course. Physics is offered every other year and she is in it. Broadband drops in the evening. A counselor meets monthly.
wellbeing: Worry about leaving home shows up as poor sleep before trips. A counselor helps her plan a short visit rather than a full move. Worry is separate from how she handles a circuit.
motivation: Make a failed circuit repeat
Learn past what the high school offers
Stay connected to home while trying a campus
strengths: Logs a connection until the test repeats
Stays with a kit when the tutorial buffers
Developing: using a computer for anything but the circuit log
workContext: Bench in a quiet room, self-paced, mostly solo. Spotty internet has to be assumed. She wants a campus that allows weekend trips home. No mobility limit.
constraints: Worry about living away from the ranch
narrative: Elise orders low-voltage kits by mail because the high school has no electronics course, and she logs each failed connection until the buzzer circuit repeats. Evenings are quiet on the ranch after chores. Spotty broadband makes tutorials stall, which frustrates her more than the wiring. A counselor helps with worry about leaving home. She hopes a bachelor's is possible with aid and is unsure she would like computing if it stayed only on a screen.

name: Darius Greene
household: Apartment with his father and two younger siblings. Father drives a city bus and gets home after 7. Darius runs the afternoon. After-school program snacks are free. Paid work is not expected yet; babysitting is.
school: Public middle-high campus, grade 10. He volunteers in the on-site after-school room for credit. No electronics lab in his schedule. Teachers know he may arrive right at the bell.
wellbeing: Unstated. He is tired on late-bus days and still wants the tutoring hour. No counseling relationship. Tiredness tracks the schedule.
motivation: Notice when a kid finally gets the game
Be home before his father worries
Learn whether listening is different from explaining
strengths: Switches an example after watching a face
Keeps siblings and the program hour in order
Developing: waiting before he gives the answer
workContext: Noisy multipurpose room, adaptive pace, children and one other adult. He needs to leave by 6. Quiet solo labs are unfamiliar, not forbidden.
constraints: Schedule tied to a bus shift
narrative: Darius volunteers after school, teaching a card game and switching examples when younger kids look lost. He likes noticing what helped and is still learning to wait before giving the answer. Money puzzles and circuit kits do not hold him. Two siblings rely on him until his father gets off the evening bus. He is curious about listening when a friend is upset and unsure that differs from tutoring.

name: Ren Alvarez
household: Shares an apartment with one parent and pays their own transit card from a part-time stock shift. Community college tuition is partly covered by a local grant that must be renewed. No dependents.
school: Community college, first year, plus a film-club night. High school had one media class. Critique is the main feedback. They are not in a performance troupe and decline on-camera roles.
wellbeing: Unstated. The stock shift is tiring and they still make the edit session. No counseling noted. They are direct about refusing camera work.
motivation: Land a cut so the joke reads
Stay in a program the grant can cover
Keep making work without being filmed
strengths: Revises timing after a group watches
Holds a deadline on a short piece
Developing: judging sound when no picture is attached
workContext: Edit bay, interruptible by critique, small crew, not an audience. Seated work. Daytime stock shifts limit studio hours. No access equipment.
narrative: Ren edits short films for a community college club, changing a cut until the joke lands, and refuses to appear on camera. They like the timing work and dislike rehearsing for an audience. A part-time stock shift covers transit, and group critiques are the main exposure to other people's projects. They are considering a longer media certificate if aid continues. They remain unsure whether sound design would appeal without a picture attached.

name: Andre Tillman
household: Small house with his mother. She has dialysis twice a week and he drives her. Summer porch crew wages are the main cash. A certificate program meets in the county seat, close enough to keep the rides.
school: Public high school, grade 12, finishing. Shop and a construction-trades intro. English is the class he delays. The crew lead lets him ask questions on site if he is on time.
wellbeing: Unstated for himself. He is careful with his mother's appointment calendar. No personal counseling. Site noise is managed with the crew's hearing protection.
motivation: See whether a brace will hold
Stay near his mother's appointments
Finish a short certificate without a distant campus
strengths: Builds a model and then asks about load and water
Speaks up when something looks unsafe
Developing: writing the explanation a teacher wants on paper
workContext: Job site or shop, physical, crew of a few, daylight hours around medical rides. Hearing protection already used. Desk essays are a poor fit.
constraints: Needs to stay in the county
narrative: Andre helps a crew on summer porch jobs and builds balsa bridges for shop class, asking what happens if the creek model rises. Essays and publicity do not interest him. He wants a short construction certificate near home. His mother needs rides to dialysis twice a week, which sets his schedule. He is unsure about leading a whole crew, though he will speak up when a brace looks wrong.

name: Claire Dumont
household: Both parents, comfortable house, no siblings at home. They pay for a counselor and can fund a public or modest private college. A hospital is close enough for a shadow day. No one depends on her wages.
school: Public high school, grade 12, with chemistry and biology labs. She dropped a fourth AP. Teachers accept a lighter schedule. The lab still lets her stay to rewrite control notes.
wellbeing: Sleep fell apart under a heavy course load. A counselor and fewer classes restored a workable evening. She can do careful lab work in shorter blocks. The sleep problem is not a stand-in for her interests.
motivation: Get a control to hold still
Understand how evidence guides a care decision
Keep enough sleep to stay in school
strengths: Rewrites notes when a result drifts
Reads a process until she can diagram it
Developing: telling a program what part of a shadow day she will not repeat
workContext: School lab, unhurried, small team, seated or standing. She wants predictable evenings. Patient rooms were unsteady; the lab bench was not. No mobility equipment.
constraints: Unwilling to treat bedside work as required
narrative: Claire volunteers in the school chem lab, rewriting control notes after a titration drifts, and reads about body systems at night. A shadow day interested her until the patient rooms; she liked the evidence talk and felt unsteady at bedsides. Store management and stage work do not appeal. She uses a counselor and a lighter schedule after sleep fell apart. She is unsure research training appeals if it includes direct care.

name: Noah Keller
household: Two parents and a sister in a town house. Money is comfortable enough for instrument repairs and a local college, not a distant conservatory without aid. Parents will support staying or going. No caregiving.
school: Public high school, grade 12. Band and a music-theory elective. The church lends a rehearsal room. He was made treasurer by default. The town college has practice space.
wellbeing: Unstated. Rehearsal nights are long and he still wants them. No counselor. Receipts annoy him; that is a task dislike, not distress.
motivation: Clear a muddy voicing
Keep the five-person group sounding even
Decide without being pushed to leave town
strengths: Hears a clash and rewrites the voicing
Rehearses until the group can repeat it
Developing: handing the money book to someone else
workContext: Small rehearsal room, repeated takes, a handful of players, not a large crowd. Evenings are the working hours. Desk finance is a poor fit. No access equipment.
constraints: Unwilling to keep the treasurer role
A move is optional and undecided
narrative: Noah arranges horns for a five-person church band and rewrites a voicing when the recording sounds muddy. He likes the rehearsal room and dislikes matching receipts, which he does because nobody else will. The town college has a music room he could use without moving. His parents support staying or going, and he has not decided. He is unsure arranging would still feel worthwhile if the group disbanded.

name: Lucia Ferrer
household: Lives with her aunt and a younger brother. The aunt's cleaning route is the household income, and Lucia prices jobs and watches her brother on weekends. An associate program at the nearby college is the affordable option if she stays part-time.
school: Finished high school last year with average grades. Currently not enrolled. She uses the public library for supplier sheets. Long sitting classes made her restless after a day of work.
wellbeing: Full shifts leave her restless in long classes. She does better with short blocks and a chance to stand. No diagnosis named. Restlessness follows the workday.
motivation: Make a price and a message match
Learn what it means to answer for the whole route
Avoid betting savings she does not have
strengths: Finds a fee that was not on the first quote
Rewrites a note so a customer understands it
Developing: sitting through a long class after a shift
workContext: Mix of driving, doorways, and a kitchen table for quotes. Fast when a job slips, then quiet paperwork. Weekends are for her brother. She would rather stand than sit a three-hour class.
constraints: Savings cannot fund a second crew
narrative: Lucia prices supplies for her aunt's cleaning route, comparing hidden fees and rewriting the text customers actually read. She likes making the offer clear and gets restless in long classes after a full shift. Lab science does not interest her. She watches her younger brother on weekends. A nearby associate program fits if tuition stays low. She wants accountability for the whole route and is unsure about risking savings on a second crew.

name: Shay Eldridge
household: Apartment with one parent near a public university. In-state tuition is reachable with a small grant and living at home. No siblings. The parent works days. Shay is not asked to earn the rent.
school: Public high school, grade 12. Advanced math and a library tutoring-center shift for volunteer hours. They are not on a contest team. Staff sometimes send college questions their way; Shay has not chosen a major.
wellbeing: Unstated. No support plan. They like a quiet carrel and decline loud assemblies when optional. Quiet is a preference, not a people limit.
motivation: Find whether a rule always works
Keep a record accurate
Choose a major without a contest script
strengths: Hunts a counterexample before accepting a rule
Proofreads a handout until the sequence holds
Developing: judging whether a group explanation is worth doing
workContext: Library carrel, quiet, solo, unhurried. A public campus commute from home fits. Stage and sales floors do not. No access equipment.
constraints: Wants to live at home for the first years
narrative: Shay spends lunch writing number puzzles and hunting a counterexample when a classmate claims a rule always works. They proofread the tutoring center's handouts and like that quieter task. Stage performance does not appeal. People ask Shay for college advice; Shay has not decided and dislikes being pushed toward contests. A public university is affordable in-state. Shay is unsure explaining proofs to a group would feel as good as solving them alone.

name: Naomi Peck
household: Apartment with her mother and older sister. Money is modest. The sister shares a bike to the library. A community garden plot is free. High school is next year. No one is asking her to work.
school: Public middle school, grade 8. General science only, no lab independent study. The library runs a garden hour. She can keep pots on the steps if water does not drip downstairs.
wellbeing: Unstated. No concern and no support plan. She is patient with slow plant notes and ordinary school days.
motivation: See if two cuttings diverge
Keep her own notes
Enter high school without freezing the choice
strengths: Writes measurements even when nothing seems to change
Keeps the two pots otherwise similar
Developing: using a procedure someone else wrote
workContext: Apartment steps or garden plot, slow, solo or with her sister. Bike access matters. A formal lab bench is unknown. No physical restriction.
narrative: Naomi compares two pots of tomato cuttings on the steps, writing height and leaf notes even when both look the same. She likes the wait-and-see part and has never used a lab. She does not want to perform or handle money. Her sister shares a bike to the library garden hour. She is unsure measuring would stay fun if someone else set the procedure. High school choices are still a year off.

name: Mina Cho
household: Lives with both parents and a younger brother in a two-bedroom rental. Parents work in food service and a hospital laundry; Korean is spoken at home and English at school. She helps her brother with reading most evenings. A public bachelor's would require aid they have not yet figured out.
school: Large public high school, grade 11. Literary magazine, one elective in another language, no shop classes this year. Library is reliable; home internet is shared and slow after dinner.
wellbeing: No current concern stated. No classroom accommodations. She uses the school library when the apartment is noisy.
motivation: Get a sentence's tone right
Be useful to her brother
See whether more school is worth the cost
strengths: Revising wording after a reader reacts
Keeping a source and a draft side by side
Still learning to say when a task is no longer hers
workContext: Quiet indoor table, unhurried revision, one partner or a small editorial group. No unusual physical access need.
constraints: Aid unclear for anything beyond local public college
Evening homework help reduces club time
narrative: Mina revises bilingual short scenes for the literary magazine and rewrites an example when a classmate misses the tone. Six years of piano were her parents' priority; she almost never sits down at the keyboard now. Comparing wording still holds her, and she does not know whether a language-heavy bachelor's is feasible without substantial aid or whether she would rather keep writing than teach.

name: Malik Everett
household: Lives with his grandmother in a small apartment near a bus line. She works nights at a warehouse. Money is tight; he uses a school laptop checked out overnight. An uncle sometimes lets him watch small appliance repairs on weekends.
school: Public middle school, grade 8. One applied-tech elective with shared hand tools and a few circuit kits. No advanced science section is offered at this campus.
wellbeing: Nothing stated as a current concern. He is in regular classes and stays after school when the shop is open.
motivation: See why a moving part failed
Finish something he can hold
Keep a tool promise to his uncle
strengths: Noticing when a rebuilt part moves differently
Staying with a test long enough to repeat it
Still learning to write down what he changed
workContext: Bench or garage pace, standing work, mostly solo with someone nearby to ask. Needs a bus route, not a car.
narrative: Malik stays after school to rebuild a small gear train and a flashlight circuit, then runs the same test twice when something sticks. He has not had a lab course, and he treats written explanations as optional. He likes the moment a revised piece changes the motion. He is unsure whether more shop time next year will exist, and he has no picture yet of training after middle school.

name: Elena Vasquez
household: Lives on a small family place with her mother, stepfather, and two younger cousins who stay weeknights. Spanish at home. Cash comes from seasonal work and egg sales. She does morning animal chores. A long drive separates them from the community college.
school: Small public high school, grade 10. Ag electives, limited lab equipment, a greenhouse the FFA shares. Internet at home drops when the wind is bad.
wellbeing: Often short on sleep from dawn chores and cousin pickup. No named health condition. She functions by swapping evening duty with her mother twice a week.
motivation: Keep animals fed and calm
Notice what changed in the pens
Stay close enough to help at home
strengths: Reading animal behavior during routine care
Keeping a simple chore and growth notebook
Still learning to separate a hunch from a repeated observation
workContext: Outdoor and barn settings, early start, small familiar crew. Needs schedules that allow cousin coverage. Standing and lifting are ordinary for her.
narrative: Elena compares how chicks and garden rows respond when she changes feed, shade, or watering, and she rewrites the notebook when a week looks misleading. She likes the chores themselves, not diagrams of cells. Stream trash behind the pasture bothers her enough to bag it. She can imagine a nearby associate program and does not know if the family can spare her hours.

name: Rowan Hale
household: Lives with their dad and older sister in a rented house. Dad is a night clerk; income is modest and steady. A spare room holds a borrowed speaker. They bike to school unless ice makes the road unsafe.
school: Public middle school, grade 8. Choir, a short dance unit in PE, and a keyboard the music room lends at lunch. No studio or theater program.
wellbeing: Crowded gyms make them edgy and they leave early if an exit is agreed. A counselor checks in every other week. Rehearsals in a smaller room go fine.
motivation: Feel a rhythm land
Show a scene clearly
Keep a way out of packed rooms
strengths: Adjusting movement after watching a run-through
Layering a short recording by ear
Still learning to keep written cues consistent
workContext: Small rehearsal room, moderate pace, a few known people. Needs a predictable exit and lower crowd noise.
narrative: Rowan rehearses short dramatic scenes in the music room and reworks a gesture when it reads as noise. They layer phone recordings at home, changing the beat more often than the melody. Packed gyms still shut them down even though small groups feel good. They have almost no picture of high-school electives and do not know whether they want to stay with dance, sound, or both.

name: Mateo Cruz
household: Lives with his father and sister in an apartment. Father works warehouse shifts. They share one car. Mateo plays rec soccer and tracks practice times in a notebook. A bachelor's would depend on aid and staying eligible to play.
school: Public high school, grade 10. Algebra 2, a stats-curious data unit inside math, soccer after school. Computer lab is available at lunch, not taken home.
wellbeing: No concern named. He manages a busy practice schedule and keeps grades high enough for the team.
motivation: Make a number pattern hold
See whether a practice change repeats
Stay on the team while school stays affordable
strengths: Building small surveys and reading a graph
Adjusting a drill and noting what repeats

household: Lives with both parents. Income is modest. A volunteer department two miles away lets explorers train on weekends.
school: Public grade 12, finished credits. Evening safety class at the station. No interest in the biology lab at school.
wellbeing: Knee injury. Cannot kneel for long. Can walk and do tabletop planning. No other concern.
motivation: see where a delay begins
check a plan against what would harm someone
compare an old writeup with another record
strengths: lining up times, notes, and a late delivery
asking what the response plan fails to cover
developing: handing work to someone else
workContext: Station table plus short walks, structured pace, a team with clear roles. Needs to avoid prolonged kneeling. Training has to stay near home.
constraints: Training has to stay near home
narrative: Cody walks a supervised safety drill, then compares gear checkout notes to see where the wait starts, including supplier sheets with the fees included. A stiff knee rules out long kneeling, so he plans from a table and short walks. He also checks an old fire writeup against a newspaper line. Marketing and biology labs do not appeal. He is unsure about being the person who assigns the work.
educationDescription: short training or associate nearby

name: Nia Coleman
household: Lives with her mother and a younger brother she walks home three afternoons a week. One shared phone hotspot; a station mentor lends headphones. Income is tight and uneven.
school: Large public high school senior. Elective audio club after last period; no formal recording courses. College counselor visits are booked out for weeks.
wellbeing: Often short on sleep when her mother works nights. No named condition. She uses a school counselor drop-in about twice a month and needs a quiet corner to finish edits.
motivation: Make a clip feel fair to the person recorded
Help younger volunteers follow a segment
Keep a neighborhood station on the air
strengths: Revises timing after hearing a rough cut
Explains a second example when a volunteer looks lost
Developing: keeping a written log of what she already tried
workContext: Small indoor studio, unhurried takes, a few familiar people. Needs seated work and predictable end times.
constraints: Aid would decide any further training
narrative: Nia stays after school layering interviews for the neighborhood station and revises a clip until the person sounds like themselves. She likes checking a second example with younger volunteers. Shared internet means she learns the board from one mentor, not a class. She is unsure whether more training should center sound or explaining things to teens.
educationDescription: Open to a short certificate or community college, only if aid and evening classes fit childcare for her brother

name: Eli Brandt
household: Lives on a small farm with both parents and a younger sister. Tools are plentiful; cash and town trips are not. An uncle nearby lets him use a bench saw.
school: Public 8th grade, one combined shop period and an FFA unit. The nearest hardware store is a twenty-minute ride. No art or music electives this year.
wellbeing: Unstated. He joins chores and shop without reported difficulty and has not asked for extra support.
motivation: Get a lid or latch to close evenly
Keep morning animal chores from slipping
See a repaired part move the way he expected
strengths: Sticks with a joint until the fit is even
Notices when an animal is off its usual pattern
Developing: writing down measurements instead of remembering them
workContext: Outdoor and shop settings, steady pace, mostly with one adult. Fine with noise and standing. Prefers not to present to a group.
constraints: Chore schedule before and after school
Long ride to any extra class
narrative: Eli planes scrap pine until a lid sits flush, then times a gate latch that sticks in cold weather. He feeds the animals each morning without being asked and rewrites a shop step only when a joint fails. The county offers one shop class and few trips. He does not know whether building would still interest him apart from the chores.
educationDescription: Undecided. He assumes he will keep working at home and has not looked at programs.

name: Rowan Hale
household: Lives with their father and grandmother in a rented duplex. Books and bus fare are reliable; a four-year college would need grants. No caregiving duty beyond occasional errands.
school: Public senior with history electives, debate, and a small archive internship at the town library one Saturday a month. Science labs are available but unused.
wellbeing: Migraine days a few times a month. They need dim light, a break from screens, and extended time. A nurse's pass covers this. Schoolwork stays complete.
motivation: Check where a claim came from
Hear a fair account of both sides
Leave a clearer written record than they found
strengths: Compares conflicting accounts without dropping one
Revises an essay after a reader marks a gap
Developing: stopping research in time to finish the draft
workContext: Quiet library or seminar table, self-paced reading, then a small discussion. Needs lighting control and no sudden loud spaces.
constraints: Aid determines whether they leave the county
narrative: Rowan spends Saturdays checking where a town record came from and rewriting a debate brief after someone pokes a hole in it. They like lining up both sides of a rule before picking a stance. Courses and one library archive are the exposure they have. They remain unsure whether arguing a dispute for someone else would feel different from studying the rule.
educationDescription: Bachelor is the hope if aid covers most of it. A local college start is the backup they will actually use.

name: Mei Okada
household: Lives with both parents and an older sister in a small apartment near a bus line. Parents work office jobs and track grades closely. Tutoring is available; free time is short.
school: Public 8th grade in a crowded middle school. Accelerated math, required lab science. She can use the library computers at lunch. Few arts electives fit her schedule.
wellbeing: Worries hard before tests and sometimes gets stomachaches. No diagnosis named. A counselor suggested a shorter practice set; she rarely uses it. She still attends fully.
motivation: Find whether a number rule always works
Avoid a careless mistake on a paper
Meet the standard her family expects
strengths: Hunts for a counterexample in a puzzle she invented
Keeps calculation steps in order
Developing: saying when a class feels pointless instead of just finishing it
workContext: Quiet desk, individual pace, little talking. She can share a table if nobody watches her work. No special physical access need.
constraints: Heavy homework and family grade expectations
narrative: Mei invents number puzzles on the bus and checks them until a counterexample appears. In lab she follows every step and still dislikes the work; accurate results have not made chemistry interesting. Her school offers math and required science, little else she has tried. She does not know if she likes solving puzzles or only likes getting them marked right.
educationDescription: Open. Family talks about a bachelor's later. She has not chosen a direction and does not want that decided by her math grade.

name: Mateo Ruiz
household: Lives with his mom and two younger cousins. He works weekend shifts at a car wash. The rec center coach lets him run a kids' drill hour for a small stipend. Money is tight.
school: Public senior. PE and a coaching helper elective. Shop and computer labs exist; he rarely enters them. Counselor knows he is weighing a local community college.
wellbeing: Unstated. He is physically tired after shifts but reports no health limit and plays a full practice.
motivation: See a kid repeat a move that failed last week
Keep the cousins' evening predictable
Earn the weekend paycheck
strengths: Changes a demonstration after watching a child's face
Keeps a practice order others can follow
Developing: sitting with a written plan instead of improvising every drill
workContext: Gym or outdoor field, active pace, kids and one adult partner. Fine standing and moving. Dislikes long desk blocks.
narrative: Mateo runs a kids' drill hour and changes the example when a player copies the wrong part. He still plays on the school team, though winning matters less than it did. Weekend shifts and cousin duty leave little time for other tryouts. He is unsure whether he likes coaching itself or likes being the person who already knows the drill.
educationDescription: Undecided between working and a low-cost associate program. Any campus plan depends on aid and keeping the weekend job.

name: June Pell
household: Lives with her grandparents on a gravel road. Internet is satellite and slow. A neighbor's truck is the ride to town. Money covers basics, not extra courses or travel.
school: Small public junior. One general science class, no dedicated earth or astronomy course. She keeps a notebook the teacher has not assigned.
wellbeing: Energy drops hard in the dark months and she misses optional events. No diagnosis named. Grandparents know; the school has not set up formal support. She keeps up required classes.
motivation: Compare what she saw in the sky with the map
Notice a week of weather that does not match the forecast
Have a record that is hers
strengths: Keeps a multi-week observation notebook
Sticks with a question after the first explanation fails
Developing: the math used to check a pattern, which she has barely practiced
workContext: Outdoor observing and a quiet kitchen table. Slow pace, mostly alone. Cold and long drives are hard in winter.
narrative: June keeps a sky notebook and a fence-post weather log, comparing what she sees with a library book that is often outdated. She has strong patience and almost no lab practice, so the patterns stay half-explained. School offers one general science class. She does not know whether more training would still appeal once the work left the backyard.
educationDescription: Undecided. A later science course would require a long bus ride or an online option she cannot reliably load.

name: Caleb Horst
household: Lives with his dad and stepmother. Dad keeps two small rental accounts and lets Caleb reconcile them. Household is comfortable, with a quiet room and a home computer. No caregiving.
school: Public sophomore. Accounting club, statistics elective, and ordinary labs he attends without interest. A community college sits two bus stops away.
wellbeing: Unstated. No support plan. He is in class daily and describes himself as fine.
motivation: Separate an estimate from money actually spent
Catch a receipt that does not match
Understand a graph before someone explains it to him
strengths: Reconciles a small set of receipts without rushing
Flags a sample that would mislead a club survey
Developing: telling a person the result out loud rather than only on paper
workContext: Indoor desk, steady pace, mostly solo with a check-in. No access accommodations. He avoids customer counters and loud rooms.
constraints: Limited interest in speaking with strangers about the numbers
narrative: Caleb reconciles his dad's rental receipts and designs small club surveys, checking who never got the form. He likes the moment an actual total replaces a guess. School gives him statistics and a club, and home gives him real paper. He is unsure he would want the work if it required persuading people rather than checking figures.
educationDescription: Open to a bachelor's later. He could start with a local accounting course. Cost is manageable with family help.

name: Maren Solberg
household: Lives with both parents and a brother. Family income is modest and steady. The school theater stores flats in their garage between shows. No one depends on her for care.
school: Public junior. Theater tech, a drawing elective, and a scene shop with hand tools. College reps visit twice a year. Academic classes are ordinary.
wellbeing: Loses the thread without a written checklist and has extra time on tests through a school plan. No further label used here. She finishes shows when the list is visible.
motivation: See a flat read clearly from the back row
Try a second layout before the director locks one
Be the person who fixes the thing that looks wrong
strengths: Tries several compositions before choosing materials
Builds a simple flat that matches the sketch
Developing: keeping tools and cues in order without a prompter
workContext: Scene shop and stage, busy before shows and quiet between. Small crew. She needs lists posted and a seat during long notes.
constraints: Focus drops when instructions are only spoken
Show weeks crowd out other classes
narrative: Maren paints sets and redraws how actors cross a shared space, then rebuilds a corner flat when the first one eats the light. She likes choosing materials more than memorizing lines. Shop class and two productions a year are her practice. She is unsure she would still want the work if it became drawings only, with nobody walking through them.
educationDescription: Open. An associate program in theater production is thinkable if she can live at home. A full bachelor's is a later question.

name: Andres Vidal
household: Lives with his mother, father, and grandmother. Spanish is the home language. He translates at clinics and school offices. Parents work long shifts. Income is modest; he is not paid for interpreting.
school: Public junior. Spanish literature, English, and a library aide period. A translation club meets weekly. Labs and shops are available and mostly unused by him.
wellbeing: Unstated. He is tired on appointment days and still attends. No support plan beyond teachers knowing he sometimes leaves early.
motivation: Keep a translation from losing someone's tone
Help his grandmother leave with the paper she actually needed
Be accurate when the stakes are a form, not a grade
strengths: Checks whether a sentence kept its tone in the other language
Finds the source a relative asked for in a stack of papers
Developing: writing his own pages rather than only repairing someone else's
workContext: Clinic waiting rooms and a library desk. Interruptible pace, one person at a time. Needs a seat and written backup when speech is fast.
constraints: Unpaid family interpreting several hours a week
Aid and home residence shape any campus plan
narrative: Andres compares passages in Spanish and English for relatives, then checks whether the tone survived. He also pulls the right sheet from a folder when someone is anxious and lost. School literature and a translation club are his formal practice. He is unsure he would want the work if it were only his own essays, with nobody waiting on the meaning.
educationDescription: A bachelor's is imaginable with aid. He would need to keep living at home the first year. He has not ruled out stopping after a certificate.

name: Luz Herrera
household: Lives with her parents above the family restaurant. She preps on Fridays and Saturdays. Household income is the restaurant's week. A younger cousin sometimes stays during dinner rush.
school: Public sophomore. Foods class and a business elective she tolerates. She can use the kitchen after the lunch period. No paid job outside the family place.
wellbeing: Back and feet ache after long prep shifts. She needs sitting breaks and a stool. No other condition named. Teachers allow her to stand or sit in class.
motivation: Leave a food-safety list people will actually follow
Know what is short before the dinner rush
Keep the weekend from falling on her mother alone
strengths: Revises a prep list after a missed step
Compares supplier totals including the fee at the bottom
Developing: talking with diners, which she does correctly and does not enjoy
workContext: Commercial kitchen, fast at service and slower during morning prep. Small family crew. Needs a stool and limits on hours standing.
constraints: Family income tied to the business
narrative: Luz preps the weekend service, compares invoices for hidden fees, and rewrites the cooling checklist after a near miss. She is practiced at the counter and dislikes the rush of explaining specials to strangers. Foods class matches home more than it adds new skills. She is unsure she wants kitchens at all if the paperwork, which she likes, were taken out.
educationDescription: Undecided. She could take a short food-safety course. A longer program is only realistic if the restaurant can spare her weekends.

name: Sam Keller
household: Lives with both parents on a creek property. A 4-H leader stops by monthly. Income is moderate farm work. A younger neighbor kid joins their habitat checks. No paid job.
school: Small public junior. Biology and an ag science elective. The stream site is school-approved. No advanced lab. Broadband is fair.
wellbeing: Unstated. Outdoor time is regular. No support plan and no reported limit.
motivation: See what changed in the same riffle after rain
Show a younger kid how to look without stirring the bottom
Cut trash they can actually haul out
strengths: Compares the same site across weeks
Explains a step again when the younger kid rushes
Developing: using a graph, which they avoid even when counts pile up
workContext: Creek bank and a barn table, unhurried, one partner or a kid. Fine with mud and weather. Quieter indoors than people assume; they still want company on the bank.
narrative: Sam checks the same stream bend each week, notes silt and trash, and shows a younger 4-H kid where to stand. They like the repeat visits more than the classroom diagrams. Ag science and a patient leader are the exposure. They are unsure whether a lab that never goes outside would still be worth the drive.
educationDescription: Undecided between a certificate and a bachelor's at a state campus an hour away. Cost would need a grant or living at home.

name: Devin Crowe
household: Lives with his mom in an apartment. A library laptop loan is his main computer. An older cousin sometimes debugs with him by phone. Money is tight; parts come from a discarded-electronics bin.
school: Public freshman. Intro computing once a week, no robotics team. He eats lunch in the library. Counselors know he skips group projects when he can.
wellbeing: Named social anxiety. He avoids presentations and crowded labs, works with one friend, and uses a pass to leave assemblies. Grades in solo work stay solid.
motivation: Find why a small program did something he did not expect
Make a broken circuit do the same thing twice
Have one project that is his, not a group grade
strengths: Traces a failed connection and writes the test down
Stays with a bug after the first guess is wrong
Developing: asking a librarian for help before he is stuck for a week
workContext: Quiet carrel or a corner at home, solo, self-paced. Needs a predictable exit from groups and no cold-call presentations.
constraints: Little money for parts or camps
narrative: Devin writes tiny programs on a library laptop and rebuilds a low-voltage board from the discard bin, logging each failed connection. Interest is ahead of practice; the class moves on before he finishes. He will work beside one friend and avoids being watched. He does not know whether he would like computing if it had to be a team project.
educationDescription: Open. A later bachelor's is a vague idea. Right now a free library workshop is the realistic next step.

name: Imani Brooks
household: Lives with both parents and a sister. Choir and a keyboard at church are free. Family income is modest and stable. They would need scholarships for a residential music program.
school: Public senior. Choir, piano, and a songwriting elective. A community arts center offers a Saturday workshop. Math and science are standard and not her focus.
wellbeing: Unstated. Rehearsals are the main evening activity. No reported difficulty and no support plan.
motivation: Get a harmony to match the words
Help an adult learner hear the phrase
Keep a group she likes showing up
strengths: Revises a short arrangement after singers miss the entrance
Leads a simple adult workshop without rushing
Developing: reading the theory behind a change she already hears
workContext: Rehearsal room, collaborative, moderate pace with intense concert weeks. Evenings. No access limits. She likes an audience she knows.
constraints: College cost and whether aid appears
Evening rehearsals already fill the week
narrative: Imani arranges short choir pieces and rewrites a lyric after listeners miss the point. She also runs an optional workshop for adults at church and asks what example would help. School choir plus Saturday workshops are steady practice. She is unsure she wants a campus program if it crowded out the people she already sings with.
educationDescription: A bachelor's in music is what she names, and she says plainly it depends on aid. A church-based year at home is the plan if aid falls short.

name: Patrick Keene
household: Lives with his parents. His dad runs a small equipment-repair side job that Patrick helps on Saturdays. A volunteer fire company lets explorers drill weekly. Income is middle, time is not.
school: Public senior. He takes a safety elective and basic auto. English is his weakest class. The fire hall is walking distance. College fairs confuse him more than they inform.
wellbeing: Unstated. Drill and Saturday work are physically fine. No support plan.
motivation: Know the limit of a response plan before someone is hurt
Keep Saturday repairs from coming back the same week
Stay useful in the town he already knows
strengths: Compares how a drill protects people in different spots
Tracks what changed after a part delay
Developing: writing the report afterward, which he shortens too far
workContext: Fire hall, shop, and roads. Alternating calm and urgent. Small crew. He can lift and stand. Needs clear radio checks, not open-ended discussion.
constraints: Saturday hours in the family repair work
narrative: Patrick drills with the fire explorers and checks how a plan changes when the access is blocked. Saturdays he helps time a repaired fitting and notes what the delay did to the job. He would rather run the checklist than write the story of it. He is unsure how much responsibility he actually wants once a mistake would be his alone.
educationDescription: Short training or an associate program in fire or emergency work, ideally while living at home. A bachelor's is not his current plan.

name: Marcus Fielding
household: Lives with his aunt and two cousins. He works days as a construction helper and sends money home. The crew lead lets him use offcuts. Transportation is a coworker’s truck.
school: Alternative high-school completion program, evening, three nights a week. A basic math module and no shop class. He is close to finishing the diploma he paused at 17.
wellbeing: Unstated mental health. Physically tired after shifts. He needs the class to stay in the evening. No counselor relationship beyond enrollment paperwork.
motivation: Finish the diploma without quitting the job
See a brace or form hold the way the lead described
Keep the household bills current
strengths: Assembles forms and bracing the crew will actually use
Stays on a repetitive build through a long day
Developing: measuring twice; he still guesses gaps and has to recut
workContext: Outdoor job site, early start, crew of several with a clear lead. Heavy physical work is acceptable. Evenings must stay free for class until he finishes.
constraints: Truck ride depends on a coworker
narrative: Marcus braces forms on a crew and recuts pieces when a gap was a guess. He wants the fit to be right and is still building the habit of measuring first. Night classes cover the diploma, not the trade. He is unsure whether more schooling after that would teach him anything the site is not already demanding.
educationDescription: Short training after the diploma, nights if possible. A degree is not the plan and he does not describe one.

name: Claire Dunlap
household: Lives with both parents. A grandparent died last year. Family income can cover a public university with some aid. She volunteers with an after-school homework room. No younger siblings.
school: Public senior. Psychology elective, peer-support training, and a child-development unit. Science is available. She has not taken anatomy. A counseling office at school sees her monthly.
wellbeing: Grief after her grandparent's death. She attends school fully, sees a counselor monthly, and sometimes needs a quieter room after group talks. No other condition named.
motivation: Be someone a classmate can talk to without being fixed
Notice when a child needed a different explanation
Understand her own reactions a little better
strengths: Listens and changes support after asking what helps
Reworks an explanation when a child stalls
Developing: knowing when a problem is past what she should handle
workContext: Homework room or small circle, calm pace, one person or a few children. She needs a pause option after heavy conversations. Desk labs do not appeal.
constraints: She does not want overnight travel for a program this year
narrative: Claire listens in a peer room and changes how she explains a game when a child goes quiet. A psychology class gives her names for some of that, and she is unsure they help. She has visited no clinic and does not know if symptom charts or care plans would appeal. Grief counseling supports her; she does not treat that as a job plan.
educationDescription: Open to a bachelor's with aid at a public campus. She has not committed to a major and says health training is only a question, not a plan.

name: Camila Ortiz
household: Lives with her two moms in a condo near a transit line. Household is comfortable. She has her own phone and a desk. No job and no caregiving. Weekend museum trips happen often.
school: Public freshman at an arts-leaning school. Media lab, drawing, and a student magazine. She can check out cameras. Academic load is moderate.
wellbeing: Unstated. She is socially active in small crews and reports no difficulty. No support plan.
motivation: Make a frame show what she meant
See which caption people actually understand
Spend time with the magazine crew
strengths: Tries several compositions before committing
Revises an edit when the timing feels late
Developing: writing the longer article, which she leaves thin
workContext: Media lab and city sidewalks with a small crew. Flexible pace. Comfortable transit. No physical access needs. She dislikes solitary long writing.
narrative: Camila shoots short sequences for the student magazine, swaps camera angles, and tests two captions to see what people think the piece is. Drawing club is the other half of her week. The media lab is there whenever she books it. She is unsure she cares about the message once the pictures already feel finished.
educationDescription: Open. Family can support college later. She treats that as available, not decided, and is fine staying in high-school media for now.

name: Jamal Rivers
household: Lives with his mom and two younger siblings he watches after school on weekdays. Saturday mornings he bikes to the animal shelter. Income is tight. The shelter supplies gloves and a bus token when it rains.
school: Public freshman. Life science, which he endures, and no animal course. PE is modified. A counselor knows the after-school childcare.
wellbeing: Asthma. High-pollen afternoons and heavy outdoor PE are a problem. He uses an inhaler, has a modified PE plan, and does fine at the indoor shelter kennels.
motivation: Keep the shelter dogs on their usual routine
Give his mom a predictable afternoon
Be outdoors when his breathing allows it
strengths: Notices a behavior change during routine care
Follows a feeding order without skipping a kennel
Developing: reading the science text, which he postpones
workContext: Kennels and home, routine pace, animals and a few coworkers. Needs indoor backup on high-pollen days and a schedule that ends before his siblings get home.
constraints: Little cash for camps or travel
narrative: Jamal does Saturday kennel care and watches which dog skips a meal, then tells the lead. He dislikes diagramming cells even when the chapter is about animals, and lab smells bother his asthma. Life science is his only formal course. He does not know if he likes the animals or likes being the reliable person on a quiet shift.
educationDescription: Undecided. He has not connected shelter Saturdays to any program. Any class after school collides with sibling care unless it is Saturday.

name: Nora Voss
household: Lives with both parents, both employed. Household is comfortable, with a quiet room and a transit pass. She has no job and no caregiving. A public university is affordable with modest family help.
school: Public magnet senior. Statistics, a student research seminar, and government. Shops and studios exist; she does not use them. Teachers expect a senior project.
wellbeing: Unstated. She keeps a full schedule, reports no difficulty, and has no support plan.
motivation: Know whether a count is trustworthy
See who a rule leaves out before arguing to change it
Finish a project she can defend
strengths: Checks a biased sample before trusting a graph
Compares how a school rule lands on different students
Developing: keeping the writing as plain as the table
workContext: Seminar room or library, self-paced then a small team. Quiet. No physical access needs. She does not want a customer floor or a shop.
constraints: She wants evidence in hand before she will argue
narrative: Nora designs small surveys for the school paper and checks whether the attendance chart changed because the activity changed or the counting did. She also gathers how a hallway rule treats different students before the forum. Magnet seminars give her practice and an audience. She is unsure she wants the argument itself once the table is already clear.
educationDescription: Bachelor's at a public university is feasible with family help. She has not picked a field and is leaving graduate study unmentioned.

name: Cole Brennan
household: Lives with his dad at the edge of a district. The bus ride is long. Income covers food and a shared truck. No club fees, no nearby mentor, and no siblings. Evenings are mostly unstructured.
school: Public sophomore. Required classes only. He skipped electives because nothing on the list was familiar. The counselor has met him once. Internet at home is phone data.
wellbeing: Asked directly, he says he is fine. No named concern and no support in place. He attends, stays quiet, and does not describe distress.
motivation: Get through the day without being put on the spot
Have an hour outside nobody schedules
Avoid a grade problem that would follow him home
strengths: Keeps a steady pace on a long run he chose
Shows up to required classes without reminders
Developing: naming an interest when a form asks for one
workContext: Outdoors, alone, flexible pace. A shared truck. He avoids counters, stages, and being watched while he tries something new. No stated physical limit.
constraints: Very limited money and local options
Few adults have asked what he wants
narrative: Cole runs the same dirt road and sometimes compares which stretch is easier to repeat, then stops writing it down. School electives did not grab him, and he will not guess for a form. He dislikes selling and being watched perform. Asked what he might want next year, he says he does not know yet, and that answer is the settled part.
educationDescription: Undecided. He has no plan past high school and no budget for visits. He is not opposed to later training; he cannot picture it.

name: Imani Brooks
household: Lives with her mother and grandmother in a rented duplex. Her mother works nights; money for tools is tight. Imani covers most evenings at home. A nearby shop lets her use a bench when it is slow.
school: Public neighborhood high school, senior. One woodshop elective, no advanced manufacturing equipment. College counselor visits are occasional.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated. No school support plan. She manages evening caregiving by leaving campus right after the last class.
motivation: make a lid fit
keep a useful shop habit
help at home without dropping the work she likes
strengths: revises joints until parts meet
notices material waste before a cut
developing: explaining a price without rushing
workContext: Prefers a staffed shop, steady pace, mostly solo bench work with occasional help lifting boards. No sensory access needs stated.
narrative: Imani spends weekends in a neighborhood shop fitting lids on small boxes until the corners sit flush. She likes revising a joint more than talking about the finished piece. Shop class is her strongest school tie, and a Saturday market stall taught her to price materials without liking sales talk. She is unsure whether a short cabinetmaking program is realistic if she also helps her grandmother most evenings.

name: Malik Adeyemi
household: Two parents and a younger brother in a modest house. His father coaches rec league. Sports fees are covered; college savings are small. No one in the home works in a clinic or lab.
school: Large public high school, sophomore. Gym is open late. Writing support is a study hall, not a special program. Science labs are standard.
wellbeing: Uses an inhaler before hard drills. No class restrictions. Mood and attention are unstated.
motivation: see a player get a drill
keep the Saturday clinic going
move more than sit
strengths: changes a drill after watching faces
repeats a move until it is stable
developing: writing down what he changed
workContext: Likes a gym or field, active pace, small groups of children. Fine with noise. Prefers not to sit through long lectures.
narrative: Malik coaches a Saturday youth basketball clinic and rewrites drills when younger players look lost. He tracks what makes a move easier to repeat but gets restless during written reflections. Science labs feel slow compared with the gym. He likes explaining a play more than performing for a crowd, and he has not decided whether helping kids is a lasting interest or just the team he already knows.

name: Luz Ortega
household: Lives with her aunt and two younger cousins. Household Spanish and English. Income is tight. A pickup is shared. Garden space is a strip behind the trailer.
school: Small public high school, junior. Agriculture plots exist. Advanced science is a single combined class offered every other year. Bus ride is long.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated. She is tired on weeks when cousins are sick, and teachers allow late worksheets then.
motivation: see what the beans actually do
keep the creek cleanup honest
be outdoors after school
strengths: keeps a growth notebook for weeks
notices shade and water differences
developing: asking for a lab explanation

Have a task with a clear routine

Stays with a repetitive care task

They have said they do not want to sell things or raise money. Whether any of this lasts past the visits is something they cannot tell yet.

name: Owen Briggs
household: Two-parent household, modest steady income, one younger sister. He has a trumpet because the family band expected it. The town paper lets students help with a yearly poll. College would need aid.

Finish what he started even when he would rather stop

Compares how a town rule lands on different people

constraints: Family aid needed for any campus living

What he volunteers for is the school poll: he rewrites a question when the first version nudges an answer, then graphs the unsure responses instead of dropping them. He also sits in on town meetings and asks who a parking rule burdens. He has not decided if more school should follow the poll work or simply get him out of rehearsal.

name: Paige Nolan
household: Both parents employed, comfortable house, one sibling. A finished basement holds a bench for low-voltage kits. She also keeps seedlings in a window. College is discussed; savings would not cover it all.

Grow something while also building something

Adjusts a small program when the output is not what she expected

constraints: Aid would still be required for a four-year campus

She wants further schooling in building and testing, and she knows her family would need aid to make a campus year work.

name: Luz Ortega
household: Multigenerational house beside a small orchard; parents and an uncle work the trees. She cooks with her grandmother several evenings and helps her with medications reminders. Spanish and English at home. Cash is seasonal.
school: Public high school, grade 12; environmental club, biology, and a foods class. Few AP options; a stream site is a short walk.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated.

Waste less of what the family already grows
Stay near people who depend on her

Revises a food-safety list after a kitchen mistake

constraints: Aid needed for even a nearby college

At home she compares how beans cook from the orchard store and rewrites the safety list when a step gets skipped. She does not want sales pitches or markets. A two-year program in town is the schooling she will consider, only if aid and her grandmother's evenings can both be worked out.

name: Malik Henry
household: Lives with his mother and two younger siblings in a walk-up. He works weekend hours at a rec center. Transit is good; college money is not set aside. An uncle keeps neighborhood photo albums he is allowed to use.

See whether another example lands

He is unsure whether he wants to keep coaching, keep digging through records, or do both. Further school is an open question that depends on aid and who is home at night.

name: Imani Brooks
household: Both parents, younger brother, stable apartment, one car. An art teacher lends a camera on weekends. Fees for portfolio programs are out of reach this year. No one at home needs daily care.

Make a room drawing that shows how people move

narrative: Imani fills pages with alternate drawings, then shoots a short hallway sequence and nudges the cut until the pause matches the step. She also sketches two layouts for the club room, marking light and where people bunch up. Number puzzles and club treasuries leave her cold. She does not know if more school is something she wants, only that she wants more time with materials than this year's electives give her.

name: Andres Vidal
household: Shares a place with his older brother; both send money to their mother. He works early warehouse shifts. Bus pass is covered by the job. English at work, Spanish with family on the phone.

Checks a supplier note against the hidden fee

constraints: He is helping support his mother
narrative: Andres already compares delivery routes, stock counts, and what slipped after a delay, then checks whether a supplier's price still matches the spec once fees are added. He dislikes explaining goods to shoppers and has no interest in performing or in layering sound. A short certificate in records or dispatch is the schooling he is willing to consider if the shift can move. He is unsure about any longer program.

name: Jamal Carter
household: Lives with his grandparents on a small place with chickens he is expected to feed. Internet is limited to a phone hotspot. The night sky is dark. Cash for activities is scarce, and the school bus is the main ride.

At night he fills a notebook with sky positions and, on storm weeks, compares what he saw with a forecast map from school. Nobody nearby does this with him, and the school has no related club. He does not know whether the notebook is a passing habit. More schooling is not a plan he can picture yet.

name: Nora Blake
household: Lives with her father; mother is out of state. She works part-time at the public library and takes the bus. Household income covers rent and not much tuition. She has a community-college fee waiver for this term.
school: Community college, first year; history, a writing course, and an intro to legal studies. High school had a debate club she joined late.

Part-time hours cap her course load

At the library desk she reorders guides so a patron can find the document they named. She has no pull toward tools, circuits, or performance. She wants to keep comparing rules with representing someone, and she has not decided which she would actually choose. A longer degree depends on aid after this waiver year.

name: Camila Soto
household: Parents run a weekend food booth; she and a younger cousin help. Bilingual household, rental duplex, one car. Summers she braids hair for relatives who pay what they can. School year evenings are mostly free.
school: Public high school, grade 10; foods, family-and-consumer class, and Spanish for heritage speakers. No business program.

Explain an item in the buyer's words

Between rushes she explains a jar to a customer and asks what they would use it for, and at home she tries a simpler braid when a cousin says the first one tugs. Sky maps and number proofs do not hold her. A short foods or personal-care course is the only further school she pictures, if the fee stays small.

name: Diego Paredes
household: Lives with his mother in a small apartment near a bus line. No tools at home; he watches mechanism videos on a shared tablet. Income is tight. A community shop hour exists across town but is hard to reach on smoky days.
school: Public middle school, grade 8; general science and art. No wood or metal shop. Math is ordinary grade-level work.

Try a build even without a shop

Asks how a load would hit a model bridge

Bus fare for that shop is tight
narrative: Diego builds small moving linkages from cardboard and scrap, compares the motion, and swaps one part. He also draws a bridge and asks which load or trickle of water would drop it, though he has never been in a shop class. Long writing and performances do not interest him. Asthma keeps him indoors when the air is bad, which slows the only free workshop he knows. He cannot tell yet if this stays a kitchen-table habit.

name: Rio Salinas
household: Lives with their father and a younger brother, whom they watch after school. Mother calls on weekends. Household is bilingual and financially modest. A school social-worker drop-in is available; they use it for schedule questions, not crisis care.
school: Public high school, grade 11; psychology elective, peer-tutoring club, and English. Quiet in large classes, talkative in tutoring.

Stay with someone who wants to talk
Make a short guide clearer

Rewrites a tutoring sequence after a confused reply
Developing: ending a helping conversation on time
workContext: Small room, unhurried, one person or a tiny group. Evenings are partly booked by their brother. No sensory accommodations.
constraints: A bachelor's path would require aid
narrative: Rio is quiet in class and still chooses the tutoring room, where they listen first and then swap the example if a teenager stares. They revise a one-page guide until the order of steps matches what the student asked. They look after a younger brother from duty and do not treat that as the same interest. Stocks and shop tools are a no. They want more school if aid appears, and they are unsure whether helping should stay informal.

name: Emiliano Cruz
household: Two parents and a sister, modest farm income, Spanish and English. He keeps the 4-H club receipt box because nobody else wanted it. Wood shop is at school, not at home. College savings are small.

motivation: Make the receipt box match the cash
Build a box that closes
Know an estimate from an actual amount

Fits a small wooden box and rechecks the lid
Developing: explaining a money difference without getting short

narrative: Emiliano would rather reconcile the 4-H receipts than lead the meeting. He separates guesses from money actually spent and will not talk about betting on a company's future. In shop he stays late until a lid sits flat. Lab science and performing leave him cold. A nearby associate program in bookkeeping or cabinet work is the furthest school idea he will say out loud, and only if the cost stays close to what the family can add.

name: Valeria Ramos
household: Lives with both parents and a grandmother in a condo they are paying down. She has a transit pass and a magnet-school lab. Family income is middle; a university would still need aid. No caregiving shift is assigned to her.
