narrative: Valeria picks the optional chemistry practical, writes down controls, and rereads the trial when a result looks too clean. On her own she diagrams how a body process changes and joined a supervised health-science hour to ask how evidence guides care. She is unsure about hands-on patient care and has no interest in selling or performing. A bachelor's program is what she wants next, and she treats aid as a requirement, not a detail.

name: Quinn Adler
household: Lives with an aunt after their parents separated. They work box office at a community theater and rehearse there. Household budget is tight; the aunt covers rent and not lessons.

Have an audience read the movement
Revise after someone watches

Revises a scene's movement after a run-through

constraints: Low winter mood cuts morning availability
Little money for training beyond high school
narrative: Quinn layers recordings, shifts the timbre, and keeps the take that finally matches the scene they are also dancing. They rewrite a dramatic beat when the audience laugh lands in the wrong place, and they like cutting picture to the same pulse. Spreadsheets, statutes, and investment talk are things they avoid. Winter mornings are unreliable even with a counselor. Further training is an open hope they cannot price yet.

name: Sebastian Mora
household: Two parents, both working, one older sister in college. Comfortable house, his own desk, reliable internet. Family speaks Spanish and English. They can help with in-state tuition and not much beyond that.
school: Public high school, grade 11; honors precalculus, computer science, and a math team. He skips student-government and retail-class fundraisers.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated.
motivation: Find a counterexample
See how data moves through a program
Explain why a rule holds, not only that it worked once
strengths: Builds a small program and tests the odd case
Writes a number puzzle and hunts a counterexample
Developing: explaining the rule so a classmate can follow

constraints: He under-explains work to other people
narrative: Sebastian invents number puzzles, looks for a case that breaks the rule, and then traces a short program to see where an unexpected value went. He likes that work and is flat about clubs that ask him to sell, host, or watch children. Online courses gave him more than the local math team does. He wants a bachelor's program and assumes it stays in state. He is unsure he will ever enjoy explaining a proof out loud, even if he can write it.

name: Aisha Grant
household: Both parents, professional jobs, younger sister, condo they own. She is not asked to provide care. School activities and art supplies are paid for. A neighborhood nonprofit lets her poster their fundraiser.
school: Public magnet, grade 10; graphic design, intro business, and biology she takes only as a requirement. Strong club access.

Sketch a look before the event
Plan a small effort with other people
strengths: Tries two poster lines and asks how each was read
Keeps a simple budget talk tied to the fundraiser's goal
Developing: noticing when a sample of opinions is only her friends
workContext: Studio plus a planning table, upbeat pace, small team. She does not want lab or outdoor sampling work. No access needs.

She likes planning who does what and what the spending is for, and she likes drawing the piece herself. She has no interest in animal care, stream surveys, or chemistry practicals. Being accountable for a whole organization's staff and money is something she cannot judge yet. More school is undecided even though the family could help pay.

name: Marisol Vega
household: Lives with her father and two brothers down a county road. One shared car. She rides along to a volunteer auxiliary where teens do supervised drills, not interior firefighting. Family income is limited; gear is borrowed.

See where a delay started
Be trusted with a careful checklist
strengths: Compares a drill plan with what actually happened
Rechecks equipment counts after a late return

constraints: Training site is about 40 miles away
Little money for gear or fees
narrative: Marisol chooses the supervised safety drills and argues about which part of the plan actually protects people. She also compares equipment routes and what the count looked like after a truck returned late. Long essays and anything about investing money do not hold her. She wants a short training course after high school and knows the distance and the single car make that fragile. She is unsure whether she wants to direct a crew or keep a specific job on it.

name: Luz Ortega
household: Lives with her mother and grandmother on a small pecan and garden plot; Spanish is the home language; cash is tight; she watches younger cousins after school; the family shares one truck.
school: Small public 11th grade with agriculture and one woodshop period; few advanced courses; the public library van comes weekly.
wellbeing: No current concern stated. She needs a predictable afternoon because cousin care starts when the bus drops her off.
motivation: Keep family tools and boxes usable
Make food her grandmother will eat
Stay near the people who rely on her
strengths: Patient refitting until a joint works
Noticing small changes in seed trays
Developing speaking a process out loud

narrative: Luz spends weekends refitting a cedar box until the lid sits flush and logging which seed trays handle the porch heat. She likes work she can redo with her hands and food that her grandmother will actually eat. Shop class and the garden are most of what she has seen. She is unsure whether a longer program is worth leaving the cousins who rely on her after school.

name: Mateo Rivas
household: Shares an apartment with his older sister in a dense neighborhood; English at home; modest wages from a youth-center job; a community camera lab is the main equipment he can use.
school: Public 12th grade in a large high school with a shared camera lab and no dedicated sound studio; he is finishing required credits.

motivation: Get the timing of a shot to feel right
Layer sound until a scene holds
Avoid feeling judged while he learns
strengths: Revising edit timing by repeated viewing
Choosing a clearer camera angle
Developing showing rough work to anyone
workContext: Small edit bay, flexible hours, solo with one collaborator; needs a way to review work privately before any group showing.
narrative: Mateo cuts short clips for a neighborhood youth night and fusses over camera angle, edit timing, and layered sound. Praise makes him shut the laptop; a counselor helps him show cuts to one person at a time. He has used a shared school camera lab and little else. He cannot tell whether more training would feel like room to improve or another audience he wants to avoid.

name: Imani Cole
household: Lives with both parents in a modest suburban house; one parent is a city clerk; bus pass and a weekend archive internship expand what they can see; no caregiving duty.
school: Public 11th grade with student government, statistics, and a history seminar; a nearby university archive hosts them on Saturdays.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated. They use no formal support and keep a steady homework rhythm.
motivation: Check a rule against who it actually burdens
See whether a count is trustworthy
Help a lost listener find the source
strengths: Comparing source copies before arguing
Explaining a rule a second way
Developing comfort with unfinished survey results

narrative: Imani compares a city parking rule with who actually gets fined, then checks the minutes that back each claim. Student government and a weekend archive internship showed them surveys, source copies, and tense meetings. They like revising an explanation when a younger student or an adult neighbor is lost. They remain unsure whether speaking for someone in a formal dispute would feel different from arguing a fair rule.

name: Aaliyah Grant
household: Shares a rental with her older sister and helps cover evenings for a younger brother; shelter volunteer stipend and a past cashier job; little savings; town bus is unreliable after dark.
school: Town public alternative program for a leftover credit; no electives this term; a school counselor keeps a short task list.

motivation: Keep animals on a steady feeding chart
Cook a meal people will finish
Have enough energy left after a shift
strengths: Calm routine animal care
Revising a food-safety list from a real meal
Developing staying with school tasks on low days
workContext: Shelter or kitchen, moderate pace, familiar small group; needs shifts that end before her energy drops.
narrative: Aaliyah closes kennels two evenings a week and cooks Sunday meals when her sister works. Feeding charts and a food-safety list feel worth doing; cashier shifts did not. Low mood makes homework slide, and a school counselor keeps tasks shorter. She has seen the shelter, the kitchen, and retail, and she does not know what training she would ask for.

name: Diego Salinas
household: Lives with his mother and uncle in a walk-up; English at home, grandparents speak Spanish; the uncle's garage is the workshop; income is steady but modest; no regular caregiving.
school: Public 11th grade with a daily shop elective and a basic electronics board; academic classes are large; writing support is a drop-in lab he rarely uses.

Keep getting real jobs from the garage

Comparing motion before and after a change
Developing writing anything longer than a test note

He writes down each test so he can repeat it, and he likes seeing a revised part change the motion. Essays and long talks drain him. He is unsure a certificate is necessary if the garage keeps giving him real jobs, because nobody at home has used a campus workshop.

name: Priya Raman
household: Two working parents and a younger brother in a comfortable suburb; family has paid for science camps and a dance studio; high expectations and no money shortage; she does not provide family care.

motivation: Make a phrase younger dancers can copy
Hear a scene read the way she intended
Keep rehearsal from being swallowed by other people's plans
strengths: Adapting a dance explanation after watching learners
Revising a short scene from one reader's note
Developing separating her plans from family pressure

narrative: Priya rewrites a dance phrase until the younger class can copy it, and she drafts short scenes she reads aloud only to a friend. Studio time is steady; grade talk at home is not, and uneven sleep follows those evenings. She has toured science camps she did not enjoy and a strong arts wing she did. She cannot tell whether college should protect rehearsal time or meet her parents' hope for a lab major.

name: Malik Brewer
household: Lives with his dad, who does landscaping and ditch work, and his mom, who works nights; income is tight; he is expected to check the lower field; a shared old computer is the only screen.
school: County public 11th grade without a science elective this year; one agriculture unit; the county map and a rain gauge are his tools.

Keep notes his dad can use
Stay on land he already understands

Sketching where water cut the field
Developing using a source beyond his own eyes

narrative: Malik checks a rain gauge before school and sketches how the creek cuts the lower field after hard weeks. Those notes help his dad decide which ditch to clear. He has no science elective, only a shared computer and a county map. Selling, filming, and arguing rules do not interest him. He is unsure whether more school would teach him anything the field has not already made him watch.

name: Nora Ellison
household: Two parents, both employed, comfortable suburb near a courthouse and a college library; no caregiving; money for camps and books is available; graduate study would still need aid she cannot yet predict.
school: Public 11th grade with debate, a history seminar, and a language class; a 504 plan provides extra time and movement breaks.

Rewrite until a classmate can follow
Try study past a first degree if aid exists
strengths: Lining up conflicting historical accounts
Adjusting tone when a passage is translated
Developing stopping a claim when the source is thin
workContext: Quiet library or seminar table, sustained reading with movement breaks, mix of solo writing and discussion.
constraints: Aid unclear past a bachelor's degree
narrative: Nora lines up two accounts of a mill strike, asks where each record came from, and rewrites the paragraph a classmate could not follow. Debate, a history seminar, and a courthouse tour gave her practice with evidence and tone across languages in assigned passages. Extra time and short movement breaks keep long readings possible. She wants deeper study and does not know whether aid would reach a graduate path or stop at a bachelor's degree.

name: Jamal Wright
household: Lives with his uncle above a small corner shop; he closes the count three nights; money is tight and headphones are his main gear; he shares a room with a cousin.
school: Public 12th grade with a business elective and no music-tech course; he is on track to finish and has not visited a college studio.
wellbeing: No named mental health concern. He is tired on close nights and uses no formal support.
motivation: Finish a drum layer that feels right
Keep the reliable shop hours for now
Avoid being watched while he makes sound
strengths: Hearing small rhythm and timbre changes

school: Public 11th grade. Dance team and a music-composition elective. Anatomy is offered; she has not taken it. An athletic trainer is at school.
wellbeing: Knee pain after jumps on concrete. The trainer tapes the knee and limits repetitions. Long rehearsals need a sprung floor. Pain changes load, not interest.
motivation: Revise a gesture so an audience can read it
Record what makes a phrase repeatable
Keep dancing without worsening the knee
strengths: Adjusts movement after watching an audience
Tracks which warm-up helps
Developing: planning studio time when fees rise
workContext: Studio ensemble she knows, rehearsal blocks, sprung floor. Impact and concrete floors must stay limited.
narrative: Hannah rehearses phrases, changes a gesture if the audience reads it wrong, and layers a short count track to lock timing. She records which warm-up lets her repeat the phrase. Concrete floors and extra jumps aggravate her knee, so long work needs a sprung floor. Chemistry sets, code, and financial puzzles do not appeal. Studio fees already stretch the household. She is unsure a costly dance program is necessary.
educationDescription: Open. A dance bachelor is costly. Community-college dance is a backup she has not accepted.

name: Andres Molina
household: Parents and a sister in a two-flat. Dad is a custodian at a community center with a wood shop. Mom cleans offices. Modest income. Bus pass. Spanish and English at home.
school: Public 12th grade. Wood tech and geometry. No business class he wants. Shop time depends on his dad's evening shift.
wellbeing: Unstated. Dust ventilation matters to him as a work practice. No named health concern.
motivation: Make a lid close evenly
Revise a joint instead of hiding the gap
Keep shop hours if his dad's shift changes
strengths: Checks fit by feel and sight
Repeats a joint until it seats
Developing: estimating what materials will cost
workContext: Wood shop, absorbed pace, mostly solo with a teacher nearby. Dust collection. Standing and lifting are fine.
constraints: Shop hours follow his dad's shift
narrative: Andres stays after his dad's shift to fit wooden boxes, revising joints until the lid sits even. He likes the quiet shop and a teacher within earshot, not a crowd. Marketing messages, policy arguments, programs, and being onstage do not appeal. Dust collection is part of careful work he wants to own. Material money and shop hours depend on that job. He aims at short training and is unsure it stays available.
educationDescription: Short training or a community-college cabinet program if aid and shop access continue. A bachelor is not his aim.

name: Lila Hart
household: Lives with her father and younger brother in a rented duplex. Shop tools at school are her main making access. Her father covers basics; a training program would need aid or a weekend job.
school: Public 11th grade with wood shop, a short drafting elective, and no robotics lab.
wellbeing: No current concern stated. She prefers predictable shop hours and ear protection around saws.
motivation: Finish a lid that closes evenly
See an idea become a usable object
Keep projects small enough to revise
strengths: Patient joint fitting
Noticing how people move through a room
Developing: explaining a build sequence aloud
workContext: Quiet shop or studio, unhurried pace, mostly solo with occasional feedback; standing is fine, loud continuous noise is not.
constraints: Aid needed for any program beyond high school
narrative: Lila has spent two years revising wooden box joints until lids sit flush, and she sketches how light and doorways change a shared room. Precise making holds her more than grades. She is unsure whether a short shop program or staying with slower design projects fits, and she has barely tried work outside the school shop. Screens and markets do not draw her.

name: Owen Briggs
household: Lives on a small grain farm with both parents and a sister. Internet is slow. County library is a 25-minute drive. College would require aid and leaving chore coverage.
school: Small public 10th grade; general science only, no earth-science elective. He uses a personal weather notebook.
wellbeing: Unstated. Early chores are tiring in harvest weeks but he manages with a set bedtime.
motivation: Compare what the sky did with what the map said
Keep a record nobody else is keeping
Understand the home place
strengths: Steady outdoor observation
Keeping week-to-week notes
Developing: writing an explanation that is more than a list
workContext: Outdoor or mixed indoor, seasonal pace, mostly alone with a partner for trips; needs reliable transport to distant sites.
constraints: Family labor in planting and harvest
Aid required to leave the county
narrative: Owen walks the same fencerow most weeks, logging clouds, wind, and ditch water, then checks a coarse forecast when the connection holds. He likes the comparison more than the farm tasks themselves. Science class rarely leaves the textbook, so he cannot tell whether longer field study would still interest him. He skips anything that puts him on a stage.

name: Marisol Vega
household: Shares an apartment with her mother and aunt. Spanish at home, English at school and the bookstore job. Tuition for a second year depends on a fee waiver and her evening shifts.
school: Community college writing course plus a public-library language table; she finished a large high school with one journalism elective.
wellbeing: No named concern. Standing retail shifts leave her too tired for late reading, so she studies mornings.
motivation: Keep a sentence's tone when the language changes
Revise until a reader hears the scene
Earn enough to stay enrolled
strengths: Close reading across Spanish and English
Revising after feedback
Developing: finishing on a deadline she did not set
workContext: Quiet tables or a small workshop, moderate pace, solo writing with discussion afterward; no heavy lifting.
constraints: Aid and waiver needed to continue
narrative: Marisol translates short passages at a weekend language table and rewrites her own scenes after a classmate marks the flat lines. The bookstore counter pays tuition, yet explaining merchandise feels unlike checking whether a translation kept the mood. She wants the associate path to stay possible and is unsure about a later bachelor's because the cost is still unknown. Circuits and machines do not interest her.

name: Rowan Ellis
household: Lives with their mother, who works nights. A spare bedroom is a recording corner with borrowed headphones. Savings are thin; any program needs a scholarship.
school: Public 12th grade with choir, a one-semester media class, and no dance studio.
wellbeing: Anxiety makes long rehearsals hard; a school counselor helps them plan shorter sets and leave early if crowded. Mood is otherwise steady.
motivation: Change a sound until it matches the feeling
Edit timing until a clip breathes
Keep performances short enough to finish
strengths: Layering rhythm and timbre
Noticing when an edit feels late
Developing: rehearsing with other people nearby
workContext: Small studio, flexible pace, solo or one partner; needs a quiet exit and breaks, not a loud all-day set.
narrative: Rowan layers short recordings and recuts phone clips until the hit lands where they hear it. Choir used to be weekly; they still like sound, but full rehearsals stall them, so they work in pieces. They do not know whether a media course would feel like play or pressure. Rules, contracts, and markets leave them cold, and they have not tried scoring for anyone else.

name: Andres Molina
household: Lives with both parents and two siblings. His uncle's small warehouse hires him weekends. Family covers rent; he saves a little from shifts. Further school is possible with aid.
school: Graduated a comprehensive high school; took accounting-lite and no shop. Now in a gap semester.
wellbeing: Unstated. He is fine on his feet for a shift if the radio stays low.
motivation: See where a delay actually started
Keep records that match the dock
Find work that is not only the family dock
strengths: Reconciling a route after a late truck
Checking a list against what arrived
Developing: saying he wants a different task
workContext: Warehouse or office corner, steady pace, small team; no preference about standing. He dislikes being the person everyone asks.
constraints: Weekend shifts expected at the family business
Unsure he can pay tuition without working
narrative: Andres already compares delivery notes, stock counts, and what changed after a truck is late. He is accurate and bored. Planning a venture or selling to customers feels like more of the same pressure, while animals and gardens do not call him. He is honestly unsure what he would study if he left the dock, only that repeating receipts is not enough.

name: Yesenia Prado
household: Lives with her grandmother and two cousins. Spanish at home. Seasonal field work supplements a tight budget. The garden is their produce in summer. A bus reaches the high school.
school: Public 10th grade; biology is textbook-only. No chemistry lab this year. FFA meets monthly.
wellbeing: No difficulty named. Heat limits afternoon garden work; she schedules morning watering.
motivation: See which seeds actually come up
Feed the household from what she grows
Learn why one bed fails
strengths: Noticing small changes in leaves
Keeping a simple garden notebook
Developing: setting up a fair comparison, not just trying harder
workContext: Outdoor beds or a small kitchen, seasonal pace, with family; needs shade breaks and Spanish-English materials.
constraints: No lab at school this year
Money for any program is uncertain
narrative: Yesenia compares seed rows behind the house and rewrites a notebook her grandmother can follow. She wants school experiments about materials but has never run one, so interest and skill are far apart. Cooking for the cousins uses the same care with a checklist. Computers, markets, and investing do not interest her. She is unsure whether more school would stay about plants.

name: Cole Brennan
household: Two parents, both employed, one older sister in college. He has a quiet room and a family laptop. They can help with in-state tuition if he keeps grades up.
school: Public 12th grade; statistics elective and math team. Few presentations. No coding course yet.
wellbeing: Unstated. He avoids assemblies; that is preference, not a stated condition.
motivation: Check whether a graph is misleading
Find a counterexample
Understand a result before talking about it
strengths: Spotting a biased sample
Inventing small number puzzles
Developing: speaking a result without reading it line by line
workContext: Quiet desk, self-paced, mostly solo, occasional pair check. No access needs stated.
narrative: Cole designs tiny surveys for a stats elective and spends evenings breaking his own number rules with counterexamples. He likes uncertain graphs and dislikes explaining them to a class. Children, performance, and selling feel draining. A bachelor's in-state looks feasible, yet he is unsure he would still like the work if it became mostly talking. He has not tried programming.

name: Samir Ortiz
household: Lives with their mother and three younger cousins they watch after school. English and Spanish at home. Apartment is crowded. After-school pay is not an option most days.
school: Public 10th grade; large classes, an after-school homework room, no electives that fit pickup time.
wellbeing: Tired from caregiving. A school social worker helps with homework planning. No other concern stated.
motivation: Help a cousin understand a game
Change an explanation when a face goes blank
Keep the afternoon from falling apart
strengths: Reworking an example on the spot
Staying patient with younger children
Developing: keeping any record of what worked
workContext: Home or classroom, interrupted pace, with children; needs a schedule that ends before pickup.
constraints: Little time or money for extra programs
narrative: Most afternoons Samir explains a board game, watches the cousins miss the point, and tries a different example. They like that adjustment and also like rewriting a one-page guide for a neighbor. Markets, ventures, and investing feel remote and unappealing. They have almost no courses outside required classes and do not know whether helping older students would feel the same.

name: Hannah Krueger
household: Lives with both parents and a dog. Her mother drives her to a county shelter on Saturdays. Household is modest and stable; a car is shared.
school: Public 11th grade; animal-care club, PE, no anatomy elective. Dance is a community class, not school.
wellbeing: Unstated. She stops practice when a knee aches and tells the instructor.
motivation: Notice what an animal does before stepping in
Make a practice easier to repeat
Keep shelter routines calm
strengths: Careful observation of behavior
Adjusting a practice until it repeats
Developing: writing down what she changed
workContext: Shelter, barn, or practice room, moderate pace, small group or solo; needs knee-friendly floors, not constant kneeling.
narrative: Hannah volunteers at the shelter, watching before she handles feeding or walking. Separately she compares dance drills and notes what her knee will repeat, with no wish to perform. Selling, campaigns, and customer talk do not appeal. She likes the animals and the practice and is unsure whether more school would be about either one. Health courses have not come up.

name: Mateo Ruiz
household: Lives with his older sister in a small apartment. He buses to a neighborhood repair shop that lets him sort parts after school. Rent is tight; any certificate needs a grant.
school: Public 11th grade; attendance is uneven. One electronics module last year. No writing electives.
wellbeing: No mental health concern stated. He uses printed steps because lectures move too fast when he is tired from closing the shop.
motivation: Find the failed connection
Make a broken device run again
Have a skill people already ask for
strengths: Tracing a low-voltage fault
Testing a swapped part twice
Developing: showing up when the work is only reading
workContext: Bench in a small shop, steady hands-on pace, one mentor nearby; seated work is fine. Written steps help.
constraints: Needs a grant for a certificate
Irregular attendance when shifts run late
narrative: Mateo assembles practice circuits and traces bad joints at the repair shop, recording which test he repeated. He is good at that and bored by essays and history packets he rarely finishes. A short certificate looks more realistic than a long degree, if a grant appears. He does not know whether he would still like the bench if the problems were only on a screen.

name: Greta Noll
household: Lives with her father on a small dairy road. Evenings she attends town meetings with an aunt. Money is tight; a state school would need aid and someone else for morning milking.
school: Public 12th grade; student council and a government elective. No media classes. Broadband is unreliable.
wellbeing: Unstated. Long meetings are fine if she can stand and stretch.
motivation: Hear how a rule hits two households differently
Check where a claim came from
Stay useful in her town
strengths: Comparing two sides of a disagreement
Asking who was left out
Developing: stopping before she speaks for someone else
workContext: Meeting room or kitchen table, uneven evening pace, with neighbors; needs transport home after dark.
constraints: Aid needed for a residential college
narrative: Greta reads the town noise ordinance against who actually gets fined, then looks for the original vote. She likes evidence on both sides and is wary of speaking as if she represents a neighbor. Cameras, music, and editing do not interest her. A bachelor's would need aid and a plan for the cows. She is unsure she wants formal disputes rather than rule discussions.

name: Eli Yellowtail
household: Lives with his mother and grandfather near a reservation town. They haul water when the pump fails. Extended family shares a truck. Programs off the reservation would need a sponsor and housing.
school: Tribal-grant public 10th grade; outdoor science days a few times a year, no lab bench of his own.
wellbeing: Unstated. Cold mornings are hard on his hands; he wears lined gloves for creek walks.
motivation: See how water moves after rain
Compare rocks and banks he already knows
Bring notes back to his grandfather
strengths: Reading terrain on foot
Remembering what a bank looked like last month
Developing: using a map scale without guessing
workContext: Outdoors along creeks, slow repeated visits, with one relative; needs a ride and gear for cold.
constraints: Housing uncertain if he studies away
narrative: Eli walks the same creek bend, lining up rock samples with a paper map and what his grandfather says the channel used to do. He wants the comparison, not a speech about it. Finance, stores, and selling feel irrelevant. School rarely gives him instruments, so he cannot tell if measuring for someone else's study would still feel like his walks.

name: Camila Soto
household: Lives with both parents and a brother. They speak Spanish and English. Her parents work days and can pay for paper and bus fare, not camps. She has a desk in a shared room.
school: Public 8th grade; art once a week, no electives yet. A phone is for family calls.
wellbeing: No concern stated. She likes to leave class a minute early to avoid the loud hall.
motivation: Try another drawing of the same idea
See whether a different material looks right
strengths: Trying several versions without freezing
Noticing color that feels wrong
Developing: deciding a piece is finished
workContext: Home desk or art room, slow pace, mostly alone; no other access needs stated.
narrative: Camila draws the same hallway in pencil, marker, and collage and keeps the one that matches the idea. That is the activity she chooses. She has not tried shops, labs, stages, or clubs long enough to know them, so most tasks stay unknown rather than disliked. She is unsure whether art will still matter next year. High school feels far, and she has no training plan.

name: Jordan Hale
household: Lives with their older sister in an apartment near a bus line. Their sister covers rent; Jordan buys groceries from a part-time library desk job. Counseling is through a community clinic on a sliding scale.
school: Public 12th grade; psychology elective and peer-helpers club. Shop classes did not fit the schedule.
wellbeing: Low mood makes mornings slow. Weekly counseling and a later start period keep them in class. They can listen in short conversations, not long shifts.
motivation: Hear what kind of support someone actually wants
Compare two explanations of the same behavior
Stay in school through this year
strengths: Listening without rushing to fix
Noticing when an example missed
Developing: keeping a boundary when a friend wants all evening
workContext: Library desk or small room, slow pace, one person at a time; needs a later start and a place to step out.
constraints: Clinic visits during some school days
narrative: Jordan stays after peer-helpers to hear someone out, then reads two explanations of why people shut down. They like the listening and dislike being handed tools or a group performance. Wood shop and mechanisms feel actively wrong, not merely unknown. A later program is possible only with aid. They are unsure about leading a group, even though one-to-one talks matter.

name: Peter Lang
household: Lives with his mother and stepfather in a townhouse. A backyard is too bright for sky notes, so he uses a park. They can fund a community-college class later, not a move.
school: Public 10th grade; algebra and a astronomy club that meets monthly. No kitchen or shop requirement.
wellbeing: Unstated. He is fine outdoors at night if a friend walks with him.
motivation: Keep a sky notebook he can trust
See why a number rule holds
Have one hobby that is his
strengths: Comparing two sky explanations
Checking a puzzle against a counterexample
Developing: staying with a page of reading that is not a puzzle
workContext: Park, bedroom desk, or club room, self-paced, solo or one club friend. No access needs stated.
constraints: Night observation needs a walking partner
narrative: Peter logs planets and bright stars, then tries to say why a number rule survives odd cases. The club is his main exposure, and he likes both activities without having lab time. Cooking, personal styling, and selling clothes do not appeal. He is unsure about college because he cannot tell whether the liking would survive a full course load. He has not asked to teach anyone.

name: Lucia Ferrer
household: Lives above her parents' small restaurant with a younger brother. Spanish in the kitchen, English at school. She preps on Fridays. Profits are uneven, so activities must be free.
school: Public 9th grade; family-consumer science once, no lab science yet. She leaves early on Fridays.
wellbeing: Unstated. Steam and long standing are tiring; she sits to finish the checklist.
motivation: Serve food that is safe as well as good
Compare ingredients when the delivery changes
Help the family night go smoothly
strengths: Revising a food-safety list
Noticing when a sauce tastes off
Developing: separating what she likes from what the restaurant needs
workContext: Small kitchen, busy dinner rush then quiet prep, with family; needs a stool and earlier nights on school days.
narrative: Lucia chooses Saturday prep, swaps ingredients when an order is short, and rewrites the cooling checklist her brother skips. She is practiced and only sometimes enjoys the rush. Cells, experiments, and formal arguments do not interest her. She cannot tell whether she wants a kitchen life or only likes feeding people she knows. School has barely offered anything else.

name: Noor Adelman
household: Lives with her father and stepmother. She uses a wheelchair. The house was partly remodeled. Family can cover community college; a distant campus would need aid and accessible housing.
school: Public 11th grade; drafting elective, elevator access, and a lab bench that is still too high. She joins design club online on bad-weather days.
wellbeing: No mental health concern. Fatigue after long transfers; she plans seated work and accessible restrooms. PE alternatives are in place.
motivation: Draw a room people can actually enter
See how a load reaches the ground
Ask users before calling a layout done
strengths: Comparing access, light, and paths
Building a small model and noting the weak joint
Developing: asking for critique without rewriting everything
workContext: Seated studio or classroom, moderate pace, small team reviews; needs step-free entry, a low bench, and nearby restrooms.
constraints: Aid if she leaves the region
narrative: Noor draws two layouts for the design-club room and builds bridge models to ask how ground and load change safety. She likes the tradeoffs and the access questions. Dance, sports drills, and stages are not appealing, and that is separate from using a wheelchair. An associate start looks feasible nearby. She is unsure about leading a crew versus staying on the drawings.

name: Kenji Watanabe
household: Lives with both parents and a younger brother in a condo they own. Parents run a small import office and expect him at the desk on Saturdays. They can pay in-state tuition. He would rather not join the firm.
school: Public magnet 12th grade; computer science and a data elective. Business club he attends only when required.
wellbeing: Unstated. He concentrates best with headphones and a written bug list.
motivation: Find why a program did something unexpected
See how data moves through a small script
Choose a path that is not the family office
strengths: Tracing unexpected program behavior
Writing down a test he can repeat
Developing: stopping a problem before it is elegant
workContext: Computer lab or bedroom, self-paced, solo with code review; headphones help. He does not want a customer floor.
narrative: Kenji writes small programs, breaks them on purpose, and checks where the data went. School has also pushed mock companies, pitches, and investing games he steadily dislikes. The skill he practices at his parents' office, sorting orders, is not the work he enjoys. A bachelor's is financially realistic. He is unsure whether computing would still appeal if the job were installing networks all day.

name: Diego Almanza
household: Lives with his parents, an uncle, and two sisters on a small cattle place. Spanish at home. Chores are daily. The school bus is long. Extra activities have to be free and local.
school: Public 8th grade; general science, no electives. 4-H meets in town once a month when the truck is free.
wellbeing: Unstated. He is used to early chores and needs a full night before the bus.
motivation: Do the animal care the right way
Watch what the calves do before moving them
Finish chores so the evening is his
strengths: Routine animal care without rushing
Noticing a calf that is off
Developing: saying what he saw in more than a few words
workContext: Pasture and barn, early pace, with family; needs gloves and a schedule that still makes the school bus.
narrative: Diego helps feed and check cattle, and he would rather watch behavior than talk about rules. The work is familiar, not a chosen club, and he has had almost no other activities to compare. Arguments, policies, and workshops do not interest him. He cannot judge desks, labs, or cities. He is unsure whether he likes the animals or likes being useful at home.

name: June Pelletier
household: Lives with her mother in a one-bedroom near a bus line. June works Sunday shifts at the library circulation desk. Her mother can help with community-college fees; a four-year school needs grants.
school: Public 12th grade; history seminar and a library-aide period. She skipped drama. Choir was one week.
wellbeing: No concern stated. She wears glasses and needs large-print handouts for long source packets.
motivation: Find the source someone actually needs
Check where a record came from
Keep a file others can follow
strengths: Organizing references so they stay accurate
Comparing conflicting accounts
Developing: helping a rushed person without taking over
workContext: Library or archive desk, quiet steady pace, mostly solo with short public questions; large print and seated work.
narrative: June shelves requests, checks whether a clipping matches the record, and likes history arguments about where a document came from. Quiet work is not a lack of interest in people; she likes a short explanation when someone is stuck. Stages, stores, and selling do not appeal. A bachelor's needs grants she does not have yet. She is unsure about teaching a whole class.

name: Mara Ellison
household: Two parents, one a facilities tech; modest income, a basement workbench, and a borrowed set of hand planes. No caregiving. Shop class is the main hands-on option nearby.
school: Public grade 8; one woodworking elective, basic art, no engineering pathway.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated. No classroom supports. She leaves noisy assemblies early by choice and returns for shop.
motivation: See a lid finally seat
Repeat a cut until it is true
Keep a useful object
strengths: Fitting joints by feel and re-cut
Noticing when a line is off
Developing measured sketches
workContext: Indoor bench, slow pace, mostly solo, standing with breaks; no access accommodation required.
constraints: Parents expect her to keep grades ordinary
narrative: Mara spends Saturdays fitting pine lids until the gap disappears, then sketches the next joint. She likes a change she can see and does not mind repeating a cut. School offers one wood elective and little else hands-on. Drawing layouts may be only a step toward a tighter box, and she has not decided whether design itself appeals. Friends assume she will keep building; she is unsure.

name: Calvin Dreher
household: Lives with his mother and grandfather on a small grain place. Tight budget, a shared truck, and open sky. He feeds chickens before the bus; no younger siblings.
school: Consolidated public grade 10; ag science, no physics lab, a part-time weather station the science teacher checks weekly.
wellbeing: Seasonal breathing trouble outdoors on high-pollen days. He shortens field notes then and finishes them on the porch. Inhaler is with him; no other support.
motivation: Compare what the sky did with the map
Keep a record that still makes sense later
Help the morning chores stay predictable
strengths: Patient outdoor notes
Spotting a change along a fence line
Developing graph reading
workContext: Outdoor or porch pace set by weather, mostly solo with a check-in person; needs a backup indoor spot on bad-air days.
narrative: Calvin keeps a sky notebook beside the chicken chart and checks both against the county map after chores. He likes when a week of notes and a radar loop disagree, then he walks the low field to see the water. Electronics kits at school feel opaque, and he does not want them. He is unsure whether more school after high school is worth leaving the place for part of the year.

name: Yesenia Prado
household: Mother works evenings; Yesenia gets her younger brother from the after-school site three days a week. Apartment is bilingual, Spanish at home. Money is tight; a community college is on the bus line.
school: Large public grade 11; creative writing, Spanish for heritage speakers, no shop. Library is open late.
wellbeing: No named concern. Tired on caregiving afternoons; teachers accept next-morning drafts. She uses that flexibility.
motivation: Keep a sentence’s tone in both languages
Revise after a real reader
Make a hard page clearer for her brother
strengths: Hearing when a translation flattens
Reordering a short scene
Developing source checks
workContext: Quiet indoor desk or library table, moderate pace, solo writing then one reader; no sensory accommodation.
constraints: Aid would have to be figured out before any campus plan
narrative: Yesenia revises short scenes in English and checks the same paragraph in Spanish for tone, then tries the clearer version on her brother. She likes a reader’s frown more than a grade. School writing is available; tools and labs are not, and she has no wish to learn them. A four-year campus is imaginable only with aid she has not mapped. She is unsure she wants workshops with adults, not just pages.

name: Andre Colton
household: Dad and older sister share a rental near the middle school. Stable modest income. A park field is two blocks away. No one depends on Andre for care.
school: Public grade 8; PE, a beginner coding teaser he skipped, and a coach who lets him log drills.
wellbeing: Sore knee after hard cuts. He shortens plyometrics and still wants the session. Athletic trainer at school tapes it on game weeks. No other concern stated.
motivation: Find which cue makes a move repeatable
Watch a younger kid get the game
Keep practice honest when the knee complains
strengths: Adjusting a drill after one try
Plain explanations to younger players
Developing patience with written logs
workContext: Gym or field, burst then rest, small groups; needs a lower-impact option on sore days.
constraints: No specialized training facility in town
narrative: Andre rewrites his practice card when a cue fails and shows the shorter version to kids at the park. He likes the moment an explanation lands. He does not enjoy money talk or mixing classroom chemicals, and he has not tried either seriously. Logging what made a move easier is new and still clumsy. He does not know if he wants to keep coaching kids or only keep his own routine.

name: Rio Santana
household: Both parents employed; comfortable shared house, a used camera, and a computer in the den. No caregiving. A community media lab is a bus ride away on Saturdays.
school: Public grade 11; video elective, band they left, no science research option they use.
wellbeing: Loud cafeterias are hard. They edit with headphones and sit near the door in class. A 504 plan covers that; mood is unstated.
motivation: Hear a cut land on the beat
Try another angle before keeping one
Finish a short piece they would replay
strengths: Timing an edit by ear
Choosing a frame that matches a sound
Developing notes on what they changed
workContext: Small edit bay, flexible pace, solo with occasional feedback; needs quieter rooms and headphones.
narrative: Rio records hallway light, then shifts the cut until the step matches the thud. They like the replay more than the assignment. Band felt public and they stopped; drawing still helps a storyboard. Spreadsheets and selling things do not interest them, and they say so. A two-year media program is the only next step they have pictured, and even that depends on whether the lab teacher’s reference is enough.

name: Imani Beltran
household: Lives with her aunt in a walk-up. She works a weekend front desk at a neighborhood center. Income is tight. City college and a public university are both reachable if aid appears.
school: Public grade 12; civics, journalism, no arts conservatory. The center lets her sit in on tenant meetings.
wellbeing: Nothing named. She manages a full week and uses the center’s quiet room between shifts.
motivation: Hear both sides before a rule changes
Find where a claim came from
Help a meeting stay specific
strengths: Lining up two accounts of the same event
Asking who a rule leaves out
Developing shorter written summaries
workContext: Meeting rooms and a library table, steady pace, with people then alone to write; no access need.
constraints: Tuition only realistic with aid she is still comparing
narrative: Imani compares a housing-rule flyer with what neighbors say happened, then writes both versions before the tenant meeting. She likes evidence that changes her mind. Journalism class feeds that; shop and performance do not, and she opts out. Representing someone in a formal dispute interests her more than performing, yet she is unsure she wants that weight rather than the discussion itself.
