wellbeing: Often tired from the afternoon schedule. No named condition. She needs quiet homework time late and a backup adult if a sibling is sick.
motivation: Notice when a child did not follow
Try a clearer example
Be someone a sibling can talk to
strengths: Changing an explanation after watching a face
Listening without rushing the person
Developing: telling whether the new example lasted until the next day
workContext: Small room, moderate pace, children nearby, predictable end time so she can get home.
narrative: After school Camila watches two younger siblings and changes a game explanation when their faces go blank. She listens when they want to talk, and she wants to know whether a clearer example still works the next day. Circuits and money markets do not interest her. A bachelor's depends on aid and on someone else covering the afternoon. She is unsure the work would feel the same if it were not her own family.
educationDescription: bachelor only if aid and another adult cover the afternoon hours

name: Andres Quintero
household: Ranch household with his parents and an uncle. Spanish at home, English at school. The drive to town is long. Cash is tight in dry months. He is expected at feeding.
school: Rural public 10th grade, ag class, no biology lab and weak computers.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: Notice an animal that is off
Finish the ordinary care completely
Stay near the work he already knows
strengths: Catching which animal hangs back
Keeping a feeding routine steady
Developing: writing down what he noticed
workContext: Outdoors, physical, early hours, with a few family members. Long desk work and keyboards do not fit.
narrative: Andres notes which heifer hangs back at feeding and stays for the ordinary care: water, gates, and watching. Ranch work is familiar; a biology lab is not, and the school does not have one. Essays and keyboards lose him quickly. He thinks a short program near home could fit, though he is unsure what he would want it to teach. He has no wish to turn the animals into a project.
educationDescription: short training near home is the only option he can picture; still undecided what it would be

name: June Pell
household: Both parents work in offices. The household can contribute to a public university later. She has a quiet desk, a library card, and a chemistry teacher who stays after school.
school: Suburban public 10th grade with an active chemistry club and standard labs, not a research program.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: See what a material actually does
Learn why a control failed
Find how far a result can be trusted
strengths: Asking a question the lab sheet did not
Coming back after a messy trial
Developing: holding conditions still and writing them down
workContext: School lab bench, daytime, a small group, standing is fine. She wants time to repeat a test.
narrative: June signs up for every chemistry demonstration and then watches her controls slip. The surprise of a result is why she stays, even when the write-up is wrong. She has started diagramming a cell process from a library book because the steps change. Precision is the skill she does not have yet. She wants to learn how an uncertain result should limit a claim. Performing and selling do not appeal.
educationDescription: bachelor is financially realistic; field open

name: Marisol Vega
household: Lives with her mother and an aunt in a rented duplex. Her aunt cooks for a small diner. Activity money is scarce. Spanish at home. No one has mapped school after high school.
school: Town public 9th grade, general schedule, no clubs she has joined.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: Have one task that feels obvious
Avoid being put on a stage
strengths: Following a short kitchen list
Noticing food that is about to spoil
Developing: naming anything she wants to try next
workContext: Known kitchen, slow, beside her aunt. She has no picture of a large staff, a lab, or a stage.
narrative: Marisol has not found a class that pulls her. She helps her aunt plate lunches on Saturdays, compares what is about to spoil, and will redo a simple safety list, and that is the only task she asks to repeat. A stock game in class felt pointless, and she will not sing in front of anyone. Most questions get a shrug. She is not deciding a path through high school yet.

name: Owen Briggs
household: Parents and a younger brother in a house they own. Hearing aids and school captioning are already in place. Family can help with a public university if he wants one.
school: Suburban public 10th grade with an electronics elective, physics, and captioned video; oral announcements are a weak channel for him.
wellbeing: Hard of hearing. He uses hearing aids, captions, and face-visible speech. Function is full when instructions are visual; PA-only directions do not work.
motivation: Find the failed connection
Make a test someone else could repeat
Compare two explanations of the same sky
strengths: Tracing a circuit without guessing
Writing a test log he can rerun
Developing: the essay side of a lab
workContext: Bench with written steps, visual alerts instead of buzzers, solo or a small group, moderate pace.
constraints: Needs captioned or written instructions and a face he can see
narrative: Owen assembles low-voltage kits, traces a dead connection, and writes the test so he can repeat it. Captions and face-to-face speech replace PA audio, which suits the bench. On clear nights he logs sky patterns and compares two explanations without picking a winner. A small program that moves his test readings interests him. Essays do not. He thinks a bachelor's is possible and is unsure about leaving.
educationDescription: bachelor is affordable at an in-state public campus; he is unsure about leaving the suburb

name: Greer Holtz
household: Two working parents in a professional household. Savings could start a bachelor's. A later graduate degree is mentioned at home and is not funded.
school: Urban public 12th grade with newspaper, debate, and an econ elective; broad course access.
wellbeing: Public speaking brings a sharp anxiety spike. A school counselor and the debate coach know. Written briefs remain her steadier work.
motivation: Line up both sides before choosing
Check where a claim came from
See how a rule lands on different people
strengths: Comparing conflicting accounts
Writing a tight brief
Developing: entering a room without a script
workContext: Newsroom or library, mostly solo writing, then a small edit meeting. She wants notice before she has to speak.
narrative: Greer writes the newspaper brief that lines up both sides and checks where a quote came from. Live debate still spikes her anxiety, so she keeps a counselor and prefers the page. An econ-class mock portfolio held her because the risk language was slippery, not because she wants to trade. A later graduate degree is a guess that depends on money. She is unsure she would want to speak for a client rather than compare the rule.
educationDescription: bachelor is feasible; graduate study is an open later hope and the cost is unsolved

name: Luis Ortega
household: Father's contracting work is irregular; mother is a clerk. Two siblings share a walk-up. Weekend labor is expected. Spanish and English at home. Aid would matter for any program.
school: Urban public 12th grade with mural club and art; no architecture course.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: See how people move through a room
Use color so a wall reads from the street
Keep the drawing, not the dust
strengths: Sketching a second layout when the first crowds people
Choosing materials for a picture
Developing: talking with a client after the drawing is done
workContext: Studio table plus short site visits to look, not to lift. Solo drawing, then a brief conversation. Heavy masonry wears him out.
constraints: Art materials compete with household bills
Travel hopes depend on future wages
narrative: Luis draws three layouts for the same stairwell, comparing light, the turn of a wheelchair, and where people bunch up. Weekends he sets tile with his father. He is good at the grid and dislikes the dust and the repetition. Mural color studies feel like the part that is his. He has no interest in performing or in pitching a product. An associate program depends on aid, and he does not know if clients would wear him out.
educationDescription: associate if a portfolio and aid line up; otherwise open

name: Imani Brooks
household: Parents and a grandmother nearby. Household income covers a house, activities, and some college savings, not a private university. She volunteers one evening at a clinic desk.
school: Suburban public 11th grade. Health-science intro is offered next year and she has not taken it. Strong library.
wellbeing: Asthma. She carries an inhaler and skips long outdoor sprints. Ordinary school days are fine. The limit is physical and is not a guide to her interests.
motivation: Find the source a person actually needs
See how evidence is supposed to guide care
Be available when a friend wants to talk
strengths: Sorting materials so someone else can find them
Listening when a friend is upset
Developing: telling study evidence from a pamphlet's claim
workContext: Indoor desk or small office, steady pace, people one or two at a time. She needs indoor options on high-pollen days.
constraints: Outdoor exertion has to stay short
narrative: Imani volunteers at a clinic desk, sorting pamphlets and showing a visitor which source matches their question. She would try a supervised intro on how symptoms, choices, and follow-up fit evidence, and she is unsure about hands-on patient care. Friends already come to her when they are upset. Asthma means she skips long outdoor runs. A bachelor's is plausible with some family help.
educationDescription: bachelor with some family help and likely aid for the rest

name: Cole Brant
household: Parents run a small-engine repair shop that covers a modest house and his Saturday pay. A training program nearby is easier to imagine than a distant campus.
school: Town public 11th grade with shop and one physics teacher who allows build projects.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: Make a revised part run better than the old one
See what a load does to a model
Know the safety limit before he skips it
strengths: Comparing a replacement part with the last one
Asking what the ground under a model would do
Developing: writing the reason, not only the fix
workContext: Shop floor, concrete pace, a few people, standing and lifting are fine. He wants a supervisor for safety calls, not for every bolt.
narrative: Cole rebuilds small engines on Saturdays and tests a replacement part against the last one. In physics he built a model bridge and kept asking what the ground and the water would do to it. A supervised safety drill interested him more than the textbook. Essays and translation exercises lose him. He is confident with his hands and leans toward short training, though he wonders if routine repairs would eventually feel too settled.
educationDescription: short training, with an associate as a later maybe

name: Sable Quinn
household: Lives with their mother, a freelance designer whose months swing. Apartment, city bus, no college savings. Sable handles some of the school-store ordering.
school: Urban public 10th grade. Entrepreneurship club and a student store; chemistry is required and unpopular with them.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: See which message people actually understood
Watch a small plan meet its budget
Find out whether leading is different from doing their own piece
strengths: Swapping one message and watching the response
Keeping a simple fundraiser list
Developing: staying in a disagreement without freezing or pushing
workContext: Busy school hallway or store corner, short cycles, people around, then a quiet recount. No access aids.
constraints: Household income changes month to month
narrative: Sable runs poster tests for the school store, swapping one message at a time to see what people think the words mean, and will explain an item if someone asks. Planning people and spending is fun until a disagreement starts, and then they are less sure. They want to compare leading that argument with just doing their own piece. Chemistry labs and the animal unit were a no. Nothing about a later path is settled.

name: Eli Harper
household: Parents and two siblings on a gravel road. Income is low. The county library is a weekly trip. A campus would require aid and a ride they do not own. 4-H is his main out-of-school group.
school: Rural public 11th grade. One environmental-science section, no statistics course. He is quiet in class.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: See what changed at the same bend
Show a younger kid the count sheet
Keep a result even when it is messy
strengths: Repeating a stream check the same way
Explaining a sample to a younger student
Developing: saying what the count cannot prove
workContext: Creek bank and a kitchen table, slow, solo work plus a few children. Large retail floors and sales talk do not fit.
constraints: No reliable ride to a campus
Family income leaves little for fees
narrative: Eli checks the same stream bend each month, writes what changed, and shows the count sheet to younger 4-H kids in a voice he never uses in class. Being quiet there is not low interest in people. Uneven samples and graphs that stay uncertain are the part he likes. Retail repels him. A bachelor's would need aid and a ride he does not have. He is unsure an indoor lab could match the bank.
educationDescription: open; a bachelor's only with substantial aid and transportation that is not secured

name: Jules Adeyemi
household: Grandmother's house. They help a younger cousin with dinner and homework several evenings. Money for travel or programs is uncertain. A dance teacher at school is the main arts access.
school: Town public 11th grade with a dance ensemble and no other advanced arts.
wellbeing: Uneven sleep and grief since a family death last year. Weekly school counselor. They function when evenings stay predictable; sudden added shifts set them back.
motivation: Make a movement readable to a viewer
Revise a phrase that did not land
Keep rehearsal as the steady hour
strengths: Revising a dance phrase after watching a viewer
Remembering a long sequence
Developing: pacing energy on low-sleep weeks
workContext: Studio with a wooden floor, rehearsal blocks, a small ensemble. They need a schedule that does not collide with cousin care.
constraints: Little money for programs away from town
narrative: Jules rehearses one dance phrase until a viewer can tell what the movement means, then changes it if the read is muddy. The ensemble is the steady part of the week. At home they help a younger cousin with dinner and homework. Since a family death, sleep is uneven and a counselor helps; evenings need to stay predictable. Money for programs away is uncertain, and so is performing for strangers outside the studio.
educationDescription: open; anything away from town needs aid that is not in hand

name: Mei Langston
household: Both parents are engineers. The house, activities, and a future bachelor's are financially comfortable. Japanese is spoken with grandparents; English is the school language. They expect the computing club to continue.
school: Suburban public 10th grade with computing club, a literary magazine, and many electives.
wellbeing: Unstated.
motivation: Revise a scene after a reader's note
Keep the tone of a line across languages
Decide for herself about the computing club
strengths: Reworking a scene's structure after feedback
Noticing when a translation changes the mood
Developing: saying no to a club she can already do
workContext: Quiet desk, long solo blocks, almost no interruptions. She does not want a noisy lab or a shop floor.
constraints: Parents expect the computing club to continue
narrative: Mei can trace a small program and fix the bug. The computing club is her parents' hope, and the satisfaction is thin. At night she rewrites a scene after one friend's note and compares how a line feels in English and in the Japanese she speaks at home. She has not told the club she wants to leave. Comfortable savings make a bachelor's easy to start and hard to aim. She does not know if the writing would hold without a grade.
educationDescription: undecided; a bachelor's is easy to pay for and hard for her to aim

name: Maya Ellison
household: Shares a two-bedroom apartment with her mother and a 12-year-old brother. Mother works nights; Maya covers weekend shifts and after-school pickup. Money is tight and steady, not crisis-level. A city bus pass and a community college nearby are the main opportunities.
school: Second-year student at a public community college, general studies, one spreadsheet elective, no lab access beyond a shared computer lab.
wellbeing: No named mental-health concern. Needs predictable evenings for sibling care; uses the campus tutoring desk for math only.
motivation: Keep family schedules from falling apart
See a plan survive a real delay
Earn without leaving the city
strengths: Rebuilding a schedule after a late bus
Noticing when a stock count does not match the shelf
Developing: reading a table without rushing the arithmetic
workContext: Indoor, moderate pace, small team with clear roles; no climbing or heavy lifting preferred.
narrative: Since junior year Maya has kept the youth-league equipment closet in order and redrawn Saturday schedules when buses run late. She likes seeing a plan hold together more than playing. Numbers on a page still slow her down, and she is unsure whether a short logistics certificate is worth missing the weekend shifts that help with rent.

name: Calvin Reed
household: Lives with both parents and a grandfather on a small grain farm. Tools and a heated shop are available; college money is not. He drives younger cousins to town on Saturdays.
school: Just finished a rural public high school. Shop and ag mechanics were the real classes; science labs were limited to kits. Nearest technical college is 40 minutes away.
wellbeing: Unstated. No support in use. Tired in planting season but not seeking help.
motivation: Make a joint close the way it should
Keep machines running through harvest
Stay close enough to help at home
strengths: Fitting wood until a lid sits even
Diagnosing a squeak by taking a part off and putting it back
Developing: writing down steps so someone else can repeat them
workContext: Shop or barn, self-paced, mostly solo with occasional help; standing and dust are fine; dislikes open offices.
constraints: Harvest and calving weeks pull him home
No spare cash for dorm living
narrative: Calvin has spent three winters fitting small boxes and resetting hinges until lids sit flush, then fixing the auger when it binds. He enjoys the wood more than the machines, though both are practiced. He is unsure whether a one-year cabinet program is worth leaving the farm during the months his grandfather still needs a second pair of hands.

name: Lydia Marsh
household: Two parents, both teachers, one younger sister. Stable income, quiet house, good library card. No caregiving load. College is expected in the family and also feels heavy.
school: Public high school, 11th grade. Honors chemistry available; she is in regular chemistry and an art elective. Lab time is short and supervised.
wellbeing: Named worry before tests that makes her leave labs early. School counselor check-ins twice a month. She still finishes written work at home.
motivation: Understand why a result changed
Avoid being rushed in front of a class
Keep the option of more school open
strengths: Writing careful lab notes when she is not timed
Asking what a control was supposed to hold still
Developing: staying in the room when a demo goes wrong
workContext: Quiet lab or library, slow pace, one partner at most; needs a seat near the door and no surprise oral quizzes.
narrative: Lydia rereads last year’s chemistry worksheets and sketches what a control was meant to keep the same, even though she rarely finishes a lab period. She likes the idea of materials more than performing them in front of others. She has almost no sense yet of whether a bachelor’s program is something she wants or only something her house assumes.

name: Rowan Hale
household: Lives with their dad and a stepfather in a rented house. One parent travels for pipeline work, so weeks alone with a dog are common. A borrowed camera and a laptop are the main tools. Income swings.
school: Public high school, 10th grade. Media elective and a small recording closet; no dance studio. Internet at home drops in storms.
wellbeing: Unstated. Prefers headphones and a predictable bell schedule. No formal support.
motivation: Get a cut to feel right
Try a sound until it matches the picture
Keep Fridays free to shoot
strengths: Choosing a camera angle and revising timing
Hearing when a layer muddies the rhythm
Developing: finishing a piece instead of restarting it
workContext: Small studio or bedroom setup, uneven bursts of work, mostly solo; needs quiet and reliable outlets, not a loud open set.
narrative: Rowan cuts short clips of the canal path and layers found sound until the timing sits right. They will rehearse a scene for a friend and then decide they would rather be behind the camera. Performing for a crowd feels unlike editing, and they do not yet know if a later media class would be about craft or about being seen.

name: Evan Cho
household: Parents run a small bakery; he lives above the shop with them and a younger sister. Evenings are dough and closing. Savings exist for a public university if he stays in-state. Grandparents visit and cook on Sundays.
school: Large public high school graduate. Took computing and one art class; skipped math team. School had a decent lab he used for assignments, not contests.
wellbeing: No difficulty stated. Sleep is short on bakery weeks. No counselor.
motivation: See how data moves when a program misbehaves
Make something people actually use at the counter
Keep Sundays for family food
strengths: Tracing a small program until the odd case shows
Sketching a screen layout people can follow
Developing: explaining a bug without sounding impatient
workContext: Mixed counter and desk, steady daytime pace, a few coworkers; fine with standing; dislikes all-night hackathons.
constraints: Closing shifts three nights a week
narrative: Evan writes small programs that track bakery preorders and then redraws the screen when his sister cannot find a button. He is good at the code and bored by contest math. Cooking with his grandparents is the part of the week he protects. He is unsure whether a bachelor’s in computing would crowd out the shop or simply make the counter easier.

name: Andre Pell
household: Lives with his aunt and two cousins in a duplex. He pays his phone and part of groceries from a rec-center job. Father is out of state. Aunt’s income covers rent; extras are his.
school: Public high school graduate, now part-time at a community college with no declared program. Took PE leadership and a basic computer class. No science lab since 10th grade.
wellbeing: Unstated. Uses the rec center as his social place. No clinical support.
motivation: Help younger kids finish a drill
Keep a gym schedule fair
Stay enrolled without dropping shifts
strengths: Changing a kids’ game explanation after watching their faces
Keeping practice on time
Developing: writing a short plan someone else can run
workContext: Gym or park, energetic pace, groups of children with one other adult; needs evening hours free; no interest in clinics or labs.
constraints: Rec-center shifts pay the phone and food share
narrative: Andre coaches a Saturday kids’ basketball hour and rewrites the drill when the eight-year-olds stop listening. He likes the explaining, not treatment or labs, and he is only average at the sport itself. Community college is a placeholder. He does not know if he wants more school or a steadier youth-program job that still lets him make rent.

name: Nora Blake
household: Lives with her mother and grandmother on a few acres. Garden and a roadside egg stand are part of household food. Father is not in contact. Broadband is a phone hotspot. College savings do not exist.
school: Small public high school, 12th grade. Ag and a family-and-consumer class; chemistry is textbook-only. Nearest community college is a county away.
wellbeing: No named concern. She is the driver for her grandmother’s appointments, which cuts into afternoons.
motivation: See which planting actually comes up
Feed people with what they grew
Stay near her grandmother
strengths: Comparing seed trays and revising the notebook
Adjusting a recipe when the stove runs hot
Developing: asking for help before a crop fails
workContext: Outdoor and kitchen, seasonal pace, family or one partner; heat is fine; long drives to campus are not.
narrative: Nora keeps a seed notebook, changes watering when one tray lags, and puts up salsa when tomatoes pile up. She likes the garden records more than any classroom science she has been offered. A certificate in horticulture sounds possible only if it does not take her off the road on the days her grandmother has appointments. She has not decided.

name: Luis Ortega
household: Both parents work hourly shifts; he is the oldest of three and sometimes watches the youngest after school. Apartment is stable. A neighbor’s dog is the animal he knows best. No college talk yet at home.
school: Public middle-to-high, 9th grade. Required science and PE only. No electives chosen. Club fair felt overwhelming and he skipped it.
wellbeing: Unstated. Quiet in class, not withdrawn at home. No support services.
motivation: Get through the school day without standing out
Spend time with the neighbor’s dog
Figure out what he even likes
strengths: Showing up and finishing assigned chores
Calming a dog on a walk
Developing: naming an interest out loud
workContext: Does not know. Prefers not to be on a stage or in a loud sales floor. Short tasks with a clear end feel safer.
constraints: After-school care for a younger sibling two days a week
narrative: Luis walks a neighbor’s dog, finishes homework when reminded, and has no club. Asked what he likes, he says animals and then goes quiet. He has not tried shops, labs, or teams long enough to judge them. He is unsure whether that blankness is a lack of interest or just no chance yet to find one.

name: Sam Keller
household: Lives with one parent, a reference librarian. Income is modest and stable. No siblings. Town historical society is walking distance. College would need aid and is discussed without pressure.
school: Public high school, 11th grade. Strong English and a thin science program. Uses captions and prefers written instructions; hearing aids in class.
wellbeing: Hearing access: needs captions, face-visible speech, and written directions. No mood concern stated. Teacher provides notes.
motivation: Check where a story came from
Hear both sides before picking one
Work from text rather than a noisy room
strengths: Comparing two accounts and noting the missing source
Keeping a citation straight
Developing: speaking up in a fast discussion
workContext: Quiet stacks or a small table, slow pace, mostly solo with written collaboration; needs captions and low background noise.
constraints: Background noise and uncaptioned video block participation
narrative: Sam spends Saturdays at the town archive comparing two versions of a mill dispute and marking where each record came from. Rules interest them when both sides are on paper. Spoken debate is harder with the room noise. They can imagine a bachelor’s with aid and still do not know if they want argument, history, or just the reading.

name: Camila Reyes
household: Lives with her mother, stepfather, and grandmother. Spanish at home, English at school. She helps with her grandmother’s evening meds and meals. Household can cover community college; a university would need grants.
school: Public high school graduate. AP Spanish and a creative writing elective. Science was average. A community college bus route exists.
wellbeing: No diagnosis stated. She gets tired from evening care and sometimes skips club meetings. A school social worker helped with aid forms.
motivation: Keep a sentence’s tone when it changes language
Be useful at home without disappearing
See if more school is actually hers
strengths: Checking whether a translation keeps the feeling
Revising an essay after one reader’s note
Developing: asking teachers for an extension before she is behind
workContext: Library or kitchen table, moderate pace, one or two people; evenings must stay free for care; no overnight travel.
constraints: Aid required for anything past community college
narrative: Camila translates short stories with her grandmother and then rewrites the English until the tone survives. She likes the language work and the revising, and she is only mildly curious about teaching. A bachelor’s is imaginable with grants. She is unsure she can carry evening care and a full campus schedule in the same year.

name: Grant Hollis
household: Two parents, one a machinist, one a payroll clerk. A garage full of parts and a patient dad. Middle income, one younger brother who does not share the shop. College is optional in this house.
school: Public high school, 11th grade. Autos and a basic electronics module. He skips DECA. Shop tools are the best-equipped part of the building.
wellbeing: Unstated. No support. Happiest with a task and a radio.
motivation: See a mechanism move the way the sketch said
Fix the thing instead of selling it
Learn a trade if the classes stay hands-on
strengths: Building a small linkage and swapping one part to test it
Staying with a repair until it repeats
Developing: reading a circuit diagram without guessing the missing wire
workContext: Garage or shop floor, steady pace, one partner; standing and noise are fine; no customer counter.
narrative: Grant builds small linkages in the garage, changes one part, and watches the motion again. Electronics class is harder; he can assemble a board and still loses the failed connection. He has no interest in selling what he fixes. A trade program sounds right, and he is unsure only about how much theory he is willing to sit through first.

name: Willa Trent
household: Lives with her father, a highway maintenance worker, in a high-desert town. Mother lives elsewhere. They share one truck. Weather station at school is student-run and underused. Money for a distant campus is not there.
school: Small public high school graduate. Earth science and a geography elective. No advanced lab. County library has maps; broadband is slow.
wellbeing: Unstated. She likes being outside for long stretches. No counseling.
motivation: Compare what the sky did with what the map predicted
Stay in country she can drive across
Find training that does not require a city
strengths: Keeping a weeks-long weather notebook
Reading terrain and where water cut the road
Developing: trusting a model when it disagrees with the porch
workContext: Field and a small office, weather-dependent pace, mostly solo or a two-person crew; needs a truck or a local posting, not a high-rise.
constraints: Aid needed to leave the county
narrative: Willa has kept a sky-and-weather notebook for two seasons and walks fence lines after rain to see where water moved soil. She likes the comparison of maps and ground more than any classroom lecture. An associate program at the county college might fit. She does not know if she would leave the high desert even if a farther school paid her way.

name: Imani Brooks
household: Lives with her mother and a cousin in a third-floor walk-up. Mother works days at a hospital cafeteria. Imani walks to a community dance studio that charges a reduced rate. Food is covered; extras are not.
school: Public arts magnet, 11th grade. Dance daily, plus a peer-tutoring period with elementary students. Science is minimal. Elevator is often out.
wellbeing: Low mood some weeks that makes morning class hard. Sees a school counselor weekly. Dance still happens on those weeks if she can start late.
motivation: Revise a phrase until the audience reads it
Help a younger kid get a game
Keep a practice that is hers
strengths: Rehearsing a scene and changing one gesture
Explaining a game again after a child freezes
Developing: getting to first period on heavy mornings
workContext: Studio or classroom, rehearsal bursts then rest, small groups; needs a building with a working elevator and a later start when mood is low.
narrative: Imani rehearses a duet until one turn reads from the back row, then on Thursdays explains a recess game to third graders and changes the words when they look lost. She wants both the dance and the kids, and she is unsure which one would still matter if a future program made her pick. Heavy mornings are real, and the counselor knows.

name: Elena Vasquez
household: Lives with both parents and an older brother in a rented flat. Parents work in food service. She has a corner desk, cheap paper, and library pencils. Brother is the one who talks about college. She does not.
school: Public high school, 9th grade. Art every day by choice. Math is a required class she completes and dislikes. No portfolio program yet.
wellbeing: Unstated. Happier drawing than talking in groups. No support requested.
motivation: Try another composition until the page feels finished
Keep art even when homework is dull
Avoid being pushed into her brother’s plans
strengths: Making several sketches and picking the one that carries the idea
Noticing how a material changes the mood
Developing: finishing a math set without resentment taking the evening
workContext: Quiet desk or art room, self-paced, mostly alone; shared tables are fine if no one watches her draw.
narrative: Elena fills sketchbooks with room layouts and faces and throws out the ones that look borrowed. She can grind through math homework because her brother checks it, and she does not enjoy a minute of that. Nobody at home has asked what training art would take. She is unsure whether she wants school after this one or just more time with paper.

name: Eli Harmon

household: Lives with their mother in a small apartment. She works two jobs. A library laptop is the computer. Rent is the priority; program fees are not.

household: Father is a mechanic and mother is a home health aide. Camila sometimes translates at appointments. Spanish and English at home. She watches homework time for neighborhood kids twice a week. Income is modest.

A bachelor program is a hope that depends on aid.

More hands-on training appeals; paying for a bachelor program is an open problem.

Sticks with a loop until the timing sits
Still learning to write down a structure someone else could follow
workContext: Small quiet room, self-paced, solo or one partner, needs volume control and a way out of crowded events
narrative: Malik layers drum recordings on a library computer and changes the timbre until the loop stops fighting itself. He will watch an edit timeline, but he refuses talent shows. School music is mostly singing in a loud room, which he avoids. Gear is borrowed. He likes the listening work and is unsure whether any class built around performing would be worth attending.

name: Aisha Trent
household: Lives with both parents and a younger cousin on weekends. The house is near a hospital she has only visited as a patient for routine care. Family income is comfortable.
school: Public middle school, grade 9 building. Elevator and extra passing time are in her plan. Peer-helping club and English are available.
wellbeing: She uses a wheelchair. Extra passing time and an elevator are the functional supports. Classes are otherwise ordinary, and mobility does not decide her interests.
motivation: Notice what explanation helps a specific person
Be taken seriously in a discussion
Keep college imaginable without rushing a choice
strengths: Listens and changes support after asking
Writes a short guide and checks if it landed
Still learning to lead a group conversation
workContext: Accessible classroom or library, moderate pace, pairs or small groups, step-free routes and nearby seating
constraints: Some club rooms are still up a flight of stairs
narrative: Aisha helps classmates redo a confusing worksheet and stays after when someone wants to talk about a bad day. She likes rewriting the example more than running the room. The school’s elevator plan lets her reach English and the library. She can imagine a bachelor’s degree. She is unsure whether preparing lessons over a whole term would appeal, or only these one-at-a-time conversations.

name: Cody Lane
household: Lives with an older brother in a rented house near a highway. Adults work rotating shifts. Activities depend on whoever is home to drive.
school: County high school, grade 9. Required courses only so far. No club has stuck. Electives start next term.
wellbeing: Unstated. No support plan and no named concern.
motivation: Get through the week without a scene
Be outside when the house is loud
Avoid picking a path before anything feels familiar
strengths: Shows up when a ride is arranged
Notices weather enough to dress and plan a walk
Has not yet practiced a skill long enough to claim it
workContext: Outdoors or a quiet corner, slow pace, alone, needs a ride home before dark
constraints: Very little money for fees or gear
narrative: Cody walks the ditch road when someone is home to unlock the house later, and sometimes writes whether the sky matched the morning. Nothing at school has lasted more than a few weeks. Most descriptions of activities draw a shrug. Driving along on a delivery once was fine. They cannot tell yet whether weather notes matter or whether next year’s elective will be the first thing they are willing to repeat.

name: Elena Vasquez
household: Lives with her father and grandmother in a small house. She volunteers at a branch library. A modest college fund covers one local year if she lives at home.

wellbeing: Migraine days need dim, predictable light and a break before screens. A school plan covers that. It does not shape what she chooses to study.
motivation: Make a record other people can rely on
Catch a biased count before someone announces it
Stay in school if the setting can be adjusted
strengths: Checks missing counts and changed definitions
Keeps a table consistent across weeks
Still learning to explain uncertainty without softening it

constraints: Aid would be required after the first local year
narrative: Elena reconciles club receipts and rechecks attendance charts when the recording method changed mid-semester. She likes finding the bias before the announcement. The magnet school gave her statistics and a library shift. A bachelor’s year at home is funded, and later years are not. She wants the checking work and is unsure she would ever want to advise another person about money they could lose.

name: Luis Ortega
household: Lives above the family bakery with his parents and an older cousin. He drives the short delivery loop on weekends. Profits are thin and shared.
school: Public high school, grade 11. Work release in the afternoon. Business math, no marketing class he respects.

motivation: Keep routes and stock from slipping
Separate the part he tolerates from the part he dislikes
Leave room for a short program that is not the counter

Keeps stock counts matched to what left the case
Customer conversation still wears him down

narrative: Luis compares Saturday delivery loops, marks which stop caused the delay, and updates the stock sheet before the case opens. He is good at that record and dislikes explaining pastries to people in line. The bakery taught him schedules, not a plan he chose. A short evening program is the only school that fits. He is unsure the routing itself appeals, or whether it only feels necessary because the family depends on it.

household: Lives with both parents, a professor and a transit planner, in a townhouse. Lab kits and museum memberships are normal. She would still need aid for a graduate plan.

Have one place that is not only chores

household: Lives with her mother and three younger cousins in a two-bedroom apartment. She handles after-school meals and homework time. Wages are hourly and variable. A neighbor covers one evening.
